item.description: In a Christchurch District Court hearing on September 22, 2026, Billie Mcfarlane was sentenced to four and a half months of home detention following a series of dog attacks that hospitalized an 11-year-old boy and his father. The incident occurred in February when the pair visited Mcfarlane's home in Christchurch. According to court testimony, the father was inside speaking with Mcfarlane while his son was in the backyard with the dogs. The dogs began barking and attacking the boy, prompting the father to run out and yell for his son. Mcfarlane attempted to control the two American Bull Staffordshire dogs but the dogs escaped into the front yard, continuing to attack the victims. Both suffered extensive injuries requiring surgery. The officer involved in the shooting was not wearing a body camera, as reported by three Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials, though a second officer had a camera turned on. item.description: The article discusses how NATO and Western non-governmental organizations (NGOs) effectively blocked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's peace-oriented mandate following his 2019 election victory. According to the author, Glenn Diesen, the 73% of Ukrainian voters who supported Zelenskiy's platform for peace with Russia faced significant opposition from Western-backed entities. item.title: US Researchers Develop AI-Powered Sensors to Detect Blockages in Nuclear Reactor Channels
item.description: A team of researchers from the US Department of Energy's Argonne National Laboratory has developed a novel monitoring system that combines fiber-optic temperature sensors with artificial intelligence to detect hidden blockages in nuclear reactors before they cause costly failures and shutdowns. The technology specifically targets heat exchangers used in molten-salt-cooled reactors (MSCRs), which contain between 2,000 and 4,000 small channels. Current monitoring systems only track temperature and flow rates at the inlet and outlet of heat exchangers, providing limited data about internal channel conditions. This new system embeds distributed fiber-optic temperature sensing into the heat exchanger's support structures, allowing for real-time temperature data collection across thousands of channels. item.title: Italian police seize €3.2 million hidden in Naples-area apartment during anti-mafia raid
item.description:
Italian anti-mafia authorities seized €3.2 million ($3.6 million) in cash from an apartment in Caivano, near Naples, during a dawn raid on Monday that resulted in the arrests of 34 people. According to the Naples Carabinieri military police, the money was concealed in multiple locations throughout the apartment, including behind wall and floor tiles, inside furniture, and in hidden wardrobe drawers. The cash consisted largely of €50 notes wrapped in cellophane and arranged in organized stacks. Officers removed the money using plastic mop buckets before transferring it to an armored vehicle.
Authorities also reported finding 11 luxury Rolex watches, weapons, and equipment allegedly associated with drug trafficking. The operation was conducted as part of a months-long investigation led by Naples anti-mafia prosecutor Nicola Gratteri. This margin is larger and more consistent than the GOP's lead at the same point in the 2022 midterms. item.description:
The article reviews Cory Doctorow’s book The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI, presenting it as an accessible examination of artificial intelligence, the technology industry’s enthusiasm around it, and the effects of AI-driven systems on workers and consumers. The review emphasizes that Doctorow does not approach AI as inherently good or bad. Instead, he is described as someone who uses AI in his own creative work and sees useful and exciting applications while also questioning the economic incentives and exaggerated claims surrounding the technology.
A central concept in the book is the “reverse centaur.” In conventional technology discussions, a centaur describes a person who combines human abilities with technology to become more productive. Doctorow uses the reverse centaur to describe workers whose jobs are transformed by technology in ways that force them to work at increasingly demanding and inhuman speeds. item.description: The German Green Party, founded in 1980 as a left-wing, ecopacifist movement, has undergone a dramatic transformation over four decades. Initially emerging from radical 1970s and 1980s movements focused on peace, ecology, feminism, and anti-nuclear activism, the Greens were known for their countercultural appearance and radical stance. They gained parliamentary representation in 1983 with 28 deputies, challenging traditional political norms with their unconventional dress and activism. The party's early years were marked by a commitment to abolishing NATO and maintaining a pacifist stance, but this shifted significantly when they joined the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in a coalition government in 1998. item.description: Cisco Talos researchers have developed a new framework called Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network (CAIRN) to identify and analyze malware that integrates artificial intelligence components. The framework was created to address the growing use of AI chatbots in cyberattacks, which has made traditional malware detection methods less effective. CAIRN identifies 'vestiges' or digital fingerprints left by AI integration in malware, allowing security teams to classify and track these threats more effectively. The researchers discovered a malware sample named CLOSEDQUORUM, which operates without human intervention by polling multiple large language models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini to determine its next actions. This malware, designed to steal login credentials and cryptocurrency, demonstrates a fully autonomous command-and-control infrastructure. item.description: The Pentagon is conducting a secret nuclear strategy review that aims to revive Cold War-era doctrines, lowering the threshold for nuclear weapons use. According to a report by Joe Cirincione published in The Bulletin on September 11, 2026, the review is being led by a small group of Pentagon officials and will not be made public. The review seeks to develop new nuclear weapons to fill every niche of the 'escalatory ladder,' effectively expanding the range of nuclear options available to the president. This approach echoes the 1950s and 1960s when the U.S. military began developing tactical nuclear weapons for battlefield use, including nuclear artillery, torpedoes, and even backpack-sized devices. item.title: The Embalmed Remains of Eva Peron: A Political and Historical Journey
item.description: Eva Peron, the iconic Argentine political figure, died on July 26, 1952, at the age of 33 from cancer. Her body was embalmed by Dr. Pedro Ara, a renowned anatomist who had learned embalming techniques from European physicians. The embalming process took place in the room where she died, with President Juan Peron granting Dr. Ara complete control and privacy. After preparation, Eva was dressed by her personal hairdresser and maid, with her nails polished and hair styled. Her casket, a fully open mahogany with a glass top, was displayed at the Ministry of Labor for public viewing until her state funeral on August 9, 1952. Millions of Argentines paid their respects during this period. Following the funeral, Dr. Ara moved her remains to a laboratory to immerse them in a chemical solution for permanent preservation, a process that continued until her monument was completed. In an interview with The New York Times, the 36-year-old congresswoman from New York discussed the complex factors influencing her decision, including her gender, ethnicity, electability, personal aspirations, and the broader progressive movement she represents.

The work is part of Stockhausen's monumental 29-hour, seven-opera cycle 'Licht,' which has never been staged in its entirety. item.title: Stem Cell Therapy Shows Promise in Restoring Motor Function After Stroke in Mice
item.description: A groundbreaking study conducted by researchers at the University of Zurich has demonstrated that stem cell transplants can reverse stroke damage and restore motor function in mice. The research, published in Nature Communications, involved the transplantation of human neural stem cells into mice that had experienced induced strokes. The transplanted cells not only survived for five weeks but also transformed into neurons that integrated with the existing brain cells, forming functional neural networks. This integration was crucial for restoring movement, as simply producing new neurons would not necessarily improve motor function. The study revealed that the stem cell treatment triggered multiple regenerative processes: new blood vessels formed in the damaged brain tissue, inflammatory processes decreased, and the blood-brain barrier's integrity improved. item.title: Smartwatches Overestimate Caloric Burn by 15-25 Percent, Study Reveals
item.description: A recent study conducted by researchers funded by the National Science Foundation has found that smartwatches commonly overestimate the number of calories burned during exercise by approximately 15 to 25 percent. The research involved 58 participants of varying ages and body weights who wore multiple smartwatches from brands including Apple, Garmin, Samsung, and Fitbit. During the study, participants also wore high-tech face masks and other scientific equipment to precisely measure metabolic changes. The findings indicate that while smartwatches are not intentionally lying about calorie counts, they consistently exaggerate the actual caloric expenditure. This overestimation could potentially lead users to make inaccurate decisions about their diet and exercise routines. The study highlights the limitations of current wearable technology in accurately tracking metabolic activity, suggesting that users should be cautious about relying solely on these devices for precise health metrics. item.description: A groundbreaking study published in the journal Nature Communications on September 15, 2026, has challenged the long-held belief that 'all roads lead to Rome' in the context of the Roman Empire's road network. The research, led by classical archaeologist Tom Brughmans from Aarhus University in Denmark, analyzed approximately 190,000 miles of Roman roads across Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. The findings reveal that Constantinople, now known as Istanbul, Turkey, emerged as a more central hub for overland travel after Emperor Constantine established it as the imperial capital in the fourth century A.D. The study's authors note that Rome was not uniquely central to the empire's road network, with provincial capitals playing significant roles in overland travel. Constantinople's strategic location between Europe and Asia made it exceptionally central to travel across the empire. item.title: Genetic changes made Kent meningitis B outbreak unusually severe, scientists find
item.description:
Scientists have identified the reason behind the unusually severe meningitis B outbreak that struck Kent in March 2026, killing two young people and hospitalizing many others. Researchers from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the University of Oxford used bacterial genome sequencing to analyze the strain responsible and discovered it had acquired genetic material from less harmful bacteria naturally present in human throats through a process called horizontal gene transfer.
This genetic exchange created a new variant that was particularly effective at causing severe illness and may have helped the bacteria evade immune detection. The outbreak, linked to a Canterbury nightclub called Club Chemistry, resulted in 21 diagnoses of invasive meningococcal disease within a single week. Two victims died: Juliette Kenny, a Year 13 pupil from Faversham, and a 21-year-old University of Kent student. Nine others required intensive care.

item.title: David George Gordon, Author and Advocate for Eating Insects, Dies at 76
item.description:
David George Gordon, a science writer who promoted insects as food, died on August 4, 2026, in a Tacoma, Washington, hospital. He was 76. His daughter, Julia Mullen Gordon, said that complications from a fall caused his death.
Gordon became widely known as the “bug chef” after publishing “The Eat-a-Bug Cookbook,” a guide that presented insects as ingredients rather than curiosities. The book included recipes and preparation methods for foods such as deep-fried tarantulas and sautéed crickets. Through his writing and energetic cooking demonstrations, Gordon encouraged Americans to reconsider their assumptions about what belongs on the dinner plate.
He also appeared on television, including “Late Night With Conan O’Brien,” where his unusual culinary demonstrations attracted both amusement and discomfort. O’Brien jokingly described him as a “freak” and “a very strange man,” reflecting the novelty of Gordon’s subject in mainstream American culture. Gordon, however, argued that the reluct

item.title: Four-Year-Old Jewish Boy Joseph Schleifstein Survived Buchenwald Concentration Camp During WWII
item.description: Joseph Schleifstein, born March 7, 1941, is one of the youngest known survivors of the Buchenwald concentration camp. His remarkable story of survival at just four years old is a testament to parental devotion, inmate solidarity, and a rare series of anomalies in the Holocaust. Born to Israel (Izrael) and Esther Szlajfsztajn in Sandomierz, Poland, during the German occupation, Joseph and his family were forced into the local Jewish ghetto in late 1942. When the ghetto was dissolved in January 1943, they were moved to the HASAG arms factory labor camps in Częstochowa, where Joseph spent over a year hidden in dark corners and crawlspaces to avoid being targeted for immediate extermination. In January 1945, as Soviet forces advanced, the family was torn apart: Joseph's mother, Esther, was deported to Bergen-Belsen, while Joseph and his father were sent to Buchenwald in Germany, arriving on January 20, 1945. item.title: A Satirical Plushie Mocks Data Center Culture with Industrial Noise
item.description: The article introduces Bezzy, a satirical plush toy created by creative agency Basura and musician Big Data. Bezzy is designed as a 'cuddly plush abomination' shaped like an industrial data center, mocking the environmental impact of server farms. The plushie is part of an 'Adopt a Data Center' campaign, parodying the WWF's 'Adopt a Panda' initiative. When hugged, Bezzy emits a loud industrial screech recorded from a Virginia neighborhood, with the tagline 'Hug me for ear piercing forever hum.' The article describes Bezzy as 'the ultimate sleep-paralysis plushie,' combining 'simulated chronic tinnitus and the ambient drone of GPUs generating AI slop, all wrapped in grey fabric.' Only 20 units were produced, and the article humorously warns that 'nothing tanks your living room's property value quite like squeezing a screaming server farm to sleep.' item.title: MIT Overtakes Princeton as No. 1 in U.S. News College Rankings
item.description:
The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has claimed the top spot in the U.S. News & World Report college rankings, ending Princeton University's 15-year reign at No. 1. The announcement, made on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, marks a significant shift in the influential but often debated rankings system that shapes perceptions of American higher education.
According to U.S. News, MIT earned the highest scores in several key metrics, including faculty research output, standardized test scores of incoming students, and post-graduation earnings. Eric Brooks, U.S. News's director of education data analysis, noted that Princeton's underlying data remained roughly stable, but the gap between Princeton and other top universities had narrowed since the publication added faculty research metrics to its formula.
The change underscores the arbitrary and shifting nature of college ranking methodologies, which many educators criticize as overly simplistic. Princeton has previously distanced itsel

item.title: Patricia Ellis: A Prominent Actress of 1930s Hollywood
item.description: Patricia Ellis (1918–1970) was an American actress who gained prominence in 1930s Hollywood through her lively performances in films produced by Warner Bros. Signed as a teenager, she was selected as a WAMPAS Baby Star in 1932, which marked the beginning of her rise from supporting roles to leading parts in light comedies and other genre films. Ellis became a familiar face in Warner Bros.' B-movie and mid-budget productions throughout the decade, often appearing alongside notable stars such as James Cagney. Known for her blonde appearance and energetic screen presence, Ellis embodied the youthful and vibrant style of 1930s popular cinema. Her career spanned the early 1930s until her retirement from acting in the early 1940s. The vintage photographs featured in this article capture the charm, energy, and classic 1930s glamour that defined Ellis's screen persona. item.title: OpenAI Establishes Mathematics Advisory Group Following AI's Resolution of Over 100 Mathematical Challenges
item.description: OpenAI has announced the formation of an independent advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence aims to provide mathematicians with greater input into the company's math-focused research. This announcement follows the publication of a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, with OpenAI claiming that its internal model has resolved more than 100 additional open problems across various mathematical fields. The group, composed of nine prominent mathematicians, will serve in an advisory capacity, assessing the significance of new results and coordinating their release. However, the group will not have decision-making power over OpenAI's research pace or direction. The Institute for Advanced Study emphasized that while the group will offer advice, it does not hold decision-making authority at any AI company, with responsibility for decisions resting solely with the company.

item.description: Major television networks, including CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, have taken decisive action in response to President Donald Trump's decision to ban their reporters from the White House. The networks filed a lawsuit in federal court on Monday, arguing that the ban constitutes an assault on press freedom and violates their First Amendment rights. The White House administration defended the ban as a necessary measure against what it described as 'an assault on the FAKE NEWS.' The networks have also coordinated to halt all video coverage of the president until further notice, signaling a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict between the Trump administration and the media. This move comes amid heightened tensions between the White House and major news outlets, with the administration accusing the media of biased reporting and the networks pushing back against what they view as an unprecedented restriction on journalistic access. item.title: Evolutionary optimization identifies corrugated airfoil designs for low-density atmospheres
item.description:
Researchers at Tokyo Metropolitan University have used evolutionary optimization and computational fluid dynamics to investigate how corrugated, insect-inspired airfoils could improve the aerodynamic performance of very small unmanned aerial vehicles in low-Reynolds-number environments. Such conditions occur in thin atmospheres, including Mars, and also affect miniature aircraft operating on Earth.
The study focused on ultra-thin, membrane-like wings. These structures are attractive for planetary UAVs because they can be lightweight and compact, while their aerodynamic behavior can resemble that of insect wings. The researchers specifically examined the effect of corrugation patterns by using a computationally idealized “zero-thickness” airfoil model. Although such an airfoil cannot be built physically, it allowed the team to isolate the influence of the corrugation geometry from effects caused by the thickness and shape of a wing’s leading edge.

item.title: Police Investigate Drug Source in Death of Model Presley Gerber, Son of Cindy Crawford
item.description: Police are investigating the possible source of drugs in the death of Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old model and son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, who died of an apparent overdose while staying at a luxury outpatient rehabilitation facility in Santa Monica. According to dispatch calls, Gerber suffered a cardiac arrest and was reported to have overdosed at Resolutions Living, a $7.7-million, seven-bedroom mansion operating as a rehabilitation home. Officers responded to the facility around 9:35 a.m. on Sunday, and paramedics pronounced him dead at 9:45 a.m. Gerber had checked into the facility just hours before, around 10 p.m. Saturday. The Los Angeles County medical examiner's office stated that the autopsy was performed but the cause and manner of death have been deferred due to ongoing testing and studies. item.title: Meta's Muse AI Agent Surpasses ChatGPT in Downloads and Faces Amazon Blocking
item.description: Meta's new AI personal agent, Muse, has surpassed ChatGPT as the top free iOS app in the U.S., with over 2.5 million downloads within less than two weeks of its launch, according to analytics firm Sensor Tower. The app, which allows users to manage and direct digital assistants that can perform tasks across the web such as filling out forms and organizing email inboxes, has outperformed competitors like Anthropic's Claude, SpaceXAI's Grok AI, and Meta's own Meta AI app. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon noted that Muse represents a shift toward broader adoption of AI agents for everyday users, a trend that contributed to Meta's stock surging over 11% on Monday. However, Muse has faced significant challenges from Amazon, which has blocked the app from accessing its platform. item.description: The article discusses a historical and philosophical analysis by Rafael Poch de Feliu, referencing French philosopher Gilles Deleuze's 1983 work 'Deux régimes de fous' (Two Regimes of Madness). This strategy, the author argues, mirrors the historical treatment of Native Americans in the United States, where indigenous populations were displaced and their existence denied. item.title: Scientists Call for Activism Over 'Hope' Amid Climate Crisis
item.description: The article 'Esperanza y derrotismo' by Rafael Poch de Feliu discusses the tension between scientific reality and the common call for 'hope' in the face of the climate crisis. The author, a scientist, reflects on a recent event at his laboratory where researchers presented their work, including data showing unprecedented environmental degradation, particularly in ocean health and planetary boundaries. The article argues that while the scientific community often emphasizes 'hope,' this approach is misleading and counterproductive. Poch de Feliu contends that the data is stark: humanity has already exceeded six of nine planetary boundaries identified 16 years ago, with two more at risk of being crossed soon, including ocean acidification. The article highlights that exceeding even one planetary boundary puts human civilization at risk, and surpassing six significantly increases the likelihood of irreversible environmental collapse. item.title: Trump Criticized for Ignoring TPS Issue During Meeting with NYC Mayor
item.description: President Donald Trump faced criticism on CNN's 'NewsNight' for not addressing a key issue during his meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The meeting, held at Gracie Mansion on Monday, was a closed-door discussion that did not result in progress on extending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for immigrants in the U.S. Mamdani later revealed during a press conference that the topic of TPS for Haitians, Syrians, and Afghans, who have fled oppression and have often worked with U.S. military forces, was not addressed during the meeting. Josh Rogin, a global security analyst for Washington Post Intelligence, condemned Trump's apparent disinterest in the matter, calling it 'unconscionable.' item.title: CDC Survey Shows Improvement in Teen Mental Health and Suicide Risk Since Pandemic Peak
item.description: A new report from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reveals encouraging progress in adolescent mental health, with significant improvements in key indicators since the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. According to the 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS), the percentage of high school students experiencing persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness dropped to 33%, down from 40% in 2023 and well below the record high of 42% in 2021. Similarly, reports of poor mental health declined from 29% to 23% over the same period. The survey also documented meaningful reductions in suicide risk behaviors: the share of teens who seriously considered attempting suicide fell from 20% to 14%, those who made a suicide plan decreased from 16% to 12%, and suicide attempts dropped from 9% to 6%. item.description: Inglewood Mayor James T. Butts Jr. held a news conference on Monday to address allegations that he inappropriately touched a high school student during a community event at City Hall. The mayor, who has served as Inglewood's leader since 2010, denied the claims and accused his political rivals of orchestrating a libelous and racist smear campaign. The incident occurred at the 'Votechella' event, where a student reportedly appeared uncomfortable as Butts pulled her close for a group photo. item.description: The Wall Street Journal's editor-at-large, Gerard Baker, has publicly diagnosed himself with a severe case of 'Trump Derangement Syndrome' (TDS), a term often used by MAGA supporters to dismiss critics of former President Donald Trump. Baker explained that he once found Trump's character and rhetoric 'repellent' but believed the nation needed transformation due to bipartisan failures and cultural shifts. item.title: British Media Outlets and Politicians Begin Criticizing Israel's Gaza Policies After 18 Months of Conflict
item.description: The article discusses a recent shift in Western media and political discourse regarding Israel's military actions in Gaza. Over the past year and a half, numerous British media outlets have published editorials condemning Israel's conduct in Gaza, marking a significant departure from previous silence or support. The Financial Times published an editorial titled 'The Shameful Silence of the West on Gaza,' criticizing the lack of condemnation from the US and Europe for Israel's actions. The Economist followed with 'The Gaza War Must End,' arguing that Trump should pressure Netanyahu to cease hostilities. The Independent and The Guardian also released strong editorials calling for an end to the conflict and urging Western nations to take action. These editorials represent a collective stance from the media organizations, not just individual opinions. Additionally, some pro-Israel figures have begun to publicly retract their support. item.title: BepiColombo Spacecraft Begins Final Approach to Mercury After 8-Year Journey
item.description: After an eight-year journey through space, the BepiColombo spacecraft is finally approaching Mercury, marking a significant milestone in planetary exploration. Launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), the probe was originally scheduled to arrive at Mercury in 2025 but faced delays due to a propulsion malfunction that required a course correction. This adjustment pushed the arrival date back by nearly a year, resulting in the spacecraft now beginning its descent to low orbit around Mercury after eight years in space. On September 3, ground control confirmed the successful separation of the propulsion module from the rest of the craft, signaling the final phase of the mission. BepiColombo has traveled approximately 6 billion miles (9.9 billion kilometers), utilizing nine gravity-assist maneuvers around Earth, Venus, and Mercury to control its velocity. item.title: Ron Johnson: Physical Retail Will Remain Strong Despite AI Shopping Trends
item.description: Ron Johnson, the former Apple retail executive who helped build Apple's iconic store network, has expressed skepticism about Silicon Valley's growing investment in AI-driven shopping experiences. In an interview with TechCrunch, Johnson argued that while AI will enhance online shopping, it won't replace the need for physical retail experiences. Johnson, who joined Apple in 2000 as the company began expanding its retail presence, emphasized that purchasing high-value items like laptops requires a tactile experience that AI cannot replicate. He stated, 'AI will never be able to have you physically experience a product,' highlighting that consumers want to feel the weight of a device, see its display, and determine the right size before making a purchase. Johnson's perspective is informed by Apple's successful retail strategy, which prioritizes human interaction and customer experience over commission-based sales. item.title: European Union's Baltic Policy Risks Escalating Tensions with Russia
item.description: The article discusses the escalating tensions between the European Union and Russia, particularly focusing on the EU's recent sanctions against Russia's 'shadow fleet' of oil tankers. The EU's 17th sanctions package, announced in May, aims to intensify pressure on Russia by restricting access to EU ports, waters, and exclusive economic zones. This policy has raised concerns about potential military confrontations between NATO, the EU, and Russia. The article highlights several incidents, including an Estonian patrol boat attempting to intercept a Russian tanker in the Gulf of Finland, which led to a Russian fighter jet overflying the Estonian vessel. Additionally, the German navy seized a Panamanian-flagged tanker, the Eventin, in the Baltic Sea after its engines failed. item.title: Understanding the Grounding-Dino Model: A Comprehensive Guide for Developers
item.description: The article provides a detailed guide to the Grounding-Dino model, a zero-shot, text-prompted object detection model maintained by Hautechai on Replicate. Grounding-Dino is based on the Grounding DINO project with a SwinT-OGC backbone, designed for open-set object detection where text prompts define detection targets without task-specific retraining. The model accepts an image and a text query containing object names, returning detected regions with bounding boxes. Key features include its ability to handle open-vocabulary queries, making it suitable for zero-shot dataset annotation, open-vocabulary image search, visual inspection prototypes, and integration with image editing workflows like Stable Diffusion and GLIGEN. The guide highlights that the model is not a segmentation or general image-understanding tool, but rather a detector that localizes objects described by language. item.title: Trump Administration Deploys Space-Based Weapons, Marking Major Shift in Space Militarization
item.description: The Trump administration has announced the deployment of weapons in orbit around Earth, marking a significant step in the militarization of space. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed this development at the Air & Space Forces Association conference, stating that the United States now possesses 'on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.' This announcement comes amid escalating tensions with nuclear-armed nations Russia and China, with Meink speaking more than six months into the US-Israeli conflict with Iran and just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping's scheduled visit to Washington. The administration has abandoned or bypassed multiple arms-control agreements, including the 2018 withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal, the 2019 exit from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the 2020 departure from the Open Skies Treaty. item.title: Australian Cannabis Tablet Shows Mixed Results in Chronic Pain Trial
item.description: An Australian-made cannabis tablet, developed by a local company, has been tested in a clinical trial involving over 150 participants as a potential treatment for chronic pain. The trial, which lasted several weeks, found the tablet to be safe for use, with approximately 10% of participants reporting some pain relief. However, the results did not show significant improvement over a placebo, meaning the tablet did not outperform a sugar pill in reducing pain levels. The tablet, which contains CBD (cannabidiol) but no THC (the psychoactive component that causes a high), was developed by TCANN, a medicinal cannabis company. CEO Peter Comerford noted that participants experienced initial pain relief within the first week, which was maintained over subsequent weeks. However, the trial design allowed participants to continue using other pain relief methods, such as paracetamol, making it difficult to determine if the CBD tablet alone was responsible for the reported improvements. item.description: The article by Rafael Poch de Feliu, published on June 18, 2025, argues that Western powers are escalating a global conflict against nations challenging their hegemony, including Russia, China, and Iran. item.description: The article discusses the recent military actions by the United States and Israel against Iran, highlighting the complex geopolitical implications. item.description: The Los Angeles Times reports on the settlement reached between California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Paramount Skydance regarding the $111-billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. The settlement, while not fully meeting California's initial demands, represents a significant victory for state-level antitrust enforcement. Under the agreement, the new Paramount mega-studio must release 30-32 films annually over five years, maintain both Paramount and Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles (preserving jobs), spend at least $1.5 billion on U.S. production over five years, and increase spending if federal or state tax credits become available. item.description: Scientists from the Technical University of Denmark, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a flexible, needle-thin brain implant capable of recording neural activity, delivering drugs, and stimulating multiple brain regions simultaneously. The device, named the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), is made from soft, plastic-like optical fibers with a specially angled tip, making it less invasive than traditional silicon-based implants. The mAxialtrode features a light-conducting core surrounded by eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids and hold thin metal wires for electrical activity measurement. item.description: On Friday, September 21, 2026, a heated exchange occurred on CNN's 'The Source' between host Kaitlan Collins and U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz regarding President Trump's recent decision to revoke press credentials for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. Collins challenged Waltz's assertion, stating that the president's actual justification did not align with Waltz's claims. item.description: Two Team Singapore athletes had to change their travel plans from Tokyo to Nagoya by bullet train due to Typhoon Dujuan cancelling their flight, according to a Singapore National Olympic Council (SNOC) spokesperson. item.title: Scientists Develop Simple Method to Convert Plastic Waste into Fuel Using Molten Salts
item.description: Scientists at Oak Ridge National Laboratory have developed a novel process that transforms polyethylene plastic waste into gasoline and diesel-like fuels using inexpensive aluminum-based molten salts. The method, which operates under relatively mild conditions (below 200 degrees Celsius), breaks down long plastic molecules into smaller hydrocarbons without requiring noble-metal catalysts, organic solvents, or external hydrogen. The process achieves a gasoline yield of approximately 60% and represents a significant advancement over traditional pyrolysis methods that typically require temperatures of 450-500 degrees Celsius. The research team, led by Sheng Dai and Liqi Qiu, utilized advanced analytical techniques including soft X-ray spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance, and neutron scattering to understand the chemical mechanisms involved. item.description: The Missouri Supreme Court has issued a ruling that has drawn strong criticism from legal experts regarding the 2026 midterm elections. The court ordered Missouri lawmakers to use a gerrymandered map from the 2025 midterms, which eliminated Democratic representation, even though ballots have already been distributed to voters based on the previous election map that a lower court had mandated. This decision is expected to create significant confusion during the vote-counting process. item.description: The article 'El sionismo y su destino' by Rafael Poch de Feliu critically examines the concept of Zionism and its implications for the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The author argues that Zionism, defined as the political position that considers the establishment of the State of Israel in a land already inhabited by Palestinians as not problematic, is inherently colonial, racist, and genocidal. item.title: Northern Gannet Dive Captures Bird Photographer of the Year 2026 Title
item.description: The Bird Photographer of the Year 2026 competition has been won by Henley Spiers with a dramatic photograph of a northern gannet diving for prey off the coast of Shetland, UK. The winning image, titled 'Sunball Rocket,' was selected from over 24,000 entries in the annual contest. Spiers captured the moment when a gannet dove through a sunbeam visible from underwater, a rare occurrence in the chilly waters of Shetland where sunshine is not always guaranteed. The gannet, known for its high-speed dives reaching up to 86 kilometers per hour, has evolved specialized features to handle the impact, including muscles that lock vertebrae, air sacs for protection, and nostrils that prevent water entry. Spiers described the gannet's dualistic nature, noting how they nurture their young in nests while exhibiting fierce hunting behavior in flight. item.title: Grail Shares Jump 34% After FDA Staff Raise No Major Concerns About Galleri Cancer Test
item.description:
Shares of Grail Inc. (NASDAQ: GRAL) surged more than 34% on Monday, September 21, 2026, after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration released briefing documents ahead of a key advisory committee meeting that showed no major concerns about the company's Galleri multi-cancer blood test. The FDA's staff reviewers did not flag significant issues with the accuracy or safety of the test, which is designed to detect more than 50 types of cancer from a single blood draw, according to the documents posted before Wednesday's meeting of the Molecular and Clinical Genetics Panel of the Medical Devices Advisory Committee.
The briefing materials indicated that the agency had no outstanding questions for the external panel on analytical performance, study design, and primary safety analyses of Galleri. However, the FDA did ask advisers to discuss whether the available evidence supports characterizing the test as an 'early detection' tool. item.title: Joseph Herscher Turns Rube Goldberg Machines Into Kinetic Art
item.description:
Joseph Herscher is a kinetic artist whose elaborate contraptions transform the logic of Rube Goldberg machines into a form of performance and visual storytelling. Rather than designing devices to accomplish useful tasks as quickly or efficiently as possible, Herscher builds intricate sequences of movements that are intentionally excessive, playful, and surprising. His machines may involve rolling objects, swinging components, falling pieces, chain reactions, and carefully timed mechanical interactions, but their main purpose is to create wonder.
The article presents Herscher’s work as an example of how familiar mechanical systems can become art. His creations depend on planning, precision, experimentation, and repeated adjustments, yet they also embrace unpredictability and humor. A small object can trigger a long chain of events, making ordinary actions appear theatrical and turning cause and effect into a kind of choreography.

item.title: Demand for Transparency on Mitch McConnell's Health Amid Speculation
item.description: U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell (R-KY) has faced growing scrutiny over his health following recent speculation about his condition. The controversy began when McConnell unexpectedly disappeared from the Senate for several weeks, later explaining that he had fallen at home, lost consciousness briefly, and was hospitalized for a mild case of pneumonia. Upon his return to the Capitol, video footage showed colleagues needing to prompt him during a vote, raising concerns about his cognitive abilities. Political analyst David Pakman, host of the liberal 'David Pakman Show' on YouTube, highlighted concerns raised by Dr. John Garrison, a forensic psychologist, who suggested McConnell may be experiencing symptoms consistent with Parkinson's or dementia. Pakman emphasized the need for 'basic clarity' regarding McConnell's health, stating that the public deserves to know whether all 100 senators are fully capable of understanding and independently making voting decisions. item.title: Barcelona Climate Inaction: A Call for Accountability in Climate Policy
item.description: The article, published on July 2, 2025, by Antonio Turiel and featured on Rafael Poch de Feliu's blog, presents a strong critique of governmental inaction regarding climate change in Barcelona. Turiel accuses current and past administrations, particularly the Generalitat government and Barcelona City Council, of failing to address the escalating climate crisis despite clear scientific warnings. The author highlights alarming statistics, including a 3-degree Celsius increase in Mediterranean Sea surface temperatures since 1980, with some areas reaching 5 degrees. He points to recent extreme weather events, such as the devastating DANA storm in Valencia eight months prior, which was exacerbated by unusually warm sea temperatures that provided additional energy and moisture to the storm. Turiel also references recent studies showing a fourfold increase in global warming rates over the past decade, which are altering ocean and atmospheric circulation patterns with unpredictable consequence

item.title: Timothy Charles Pigford, Civil Rights Activist and Black Farmers Advocate, Dies at 74
item.description:
Timothy Charles Pigford, the lead plaintiff in the historic Pigford v. Glickman class-action lawsuit that exposed decades of systematic discrimination against Black farmers by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, has died at age 74. Pigford passed away on August 23, 2026, at ECU Health Beaufort Hospital in Washington, North Carolina.
Born on November 15, 1951, in Willard, North Carolina, Pigford dedicated his life to farming, civil rights activism, and historical research. His landmark 1997 litigation against the USDA resulted in one of the largest civil rights settlements in American history, with a federal court estimating the discrimination suffered by Black farmers to be worth at least $2.25 billion in restitution. The case brought national attention to the systematic denial of loans and other assistance to Black farmers that had persisted for over a century.

item.title: Chrome Extension Uses Single Stream for Real-Time Caption Translation with Improved Efficiency
item.description: The article details the development of a Chrome extension that provides real-time translated captions for video calls on platforms like Meet, Zoom, and Teams. The extension captures audio directly from the browser tab without requiring a bot to join the call, addressing challenges specific to Chrome's Manifest V3 (MV3) architecture. Key technical hurdles included handling tab audio capture in MV3, which restricts background scripts from accessing Web Audio APIs, and optimizing the translation process to reduce costs and improve efficiency. The author explains how they initially used two services (Deepgram for speech recognition and DeepL for translation), which proved expensive due to repeated translation of incomplete phrases. By switching to Soniox's stt-rt-v5 model, which combines speech recognition and translation in a single stream, the cost dropped significantly—from $2.55 per hour to $0.154 per hour. item.title: 1957 Daimler Conquest Drophead Coupé: A Rare British Convertible from the 1950s
item.description: The 1957 Daimler Conquest Drophead Coupé represents a rare and elegant British convertible from the mid-1950s, part of Daimler's Conquest range. This three-seater drophead model featured a distinctive design with a side-facing rear 'buddy' seat and stylish coachwork. Powered by a refined 2.4-litre straight-six engine producing approximately 100 horsepower in Century specification, it combined comfortable grand-touring qualities with open-top motoring. Produced in very limited numbers—only around 50 to 60 examples—the 1957 Daimler Conquest Drophead Coupé remains a highly desirable classic due to its rarity, understated luxury, and distinctive Daimler character. The vehicle's elegant photos capture the rare style and refined British charm that defined this model. As a classic automobile, it exemplifies the craftsmanship and design aesthetics of British automotive engineering during the 1950s. item.title: California Man Killed After Violent Chase Involving Stolen Guns, Forest Fires, and Murder
item.description: A 44-year-old man named Derek Spencer was killed in a shootout with Placer County sheriff's deputies on Monday morning after leading law enforcement on a violent chase across Placer County. The incident began when Spencer allegedly brandished a firearm in Placer County on Saturday, stole a car and guns, and shot at a moving car in El Dorado County. Authorities reported that Spencer rammed a patrol car and fled into a heavily forested area near Iowa Hill, about 60 miles north of Sacramento. During the pursuit, Spencer allegedly started forest fires as deputies closed in, forcing firefighters to delay their response until after the shootout. The manhunt involved multiple law enforcement agencies, including the El Dorado County Sheriff's Office, Nevada County Sheriff's Office, and the California Highway Patrol, who used helicopters, drones, and infrared technology to locate Spencer. Authorities found a woman dead inside a home in the area, which they believe Spencer shot before fleeing. S

item.title: Dragonfly Mission to Explore Hydrocarbon Dunes on Titan
item.description: The Dragonfly mission, set to launch in 2028, will explore the hydrocarbon dune fields on Saturn's moon Titan, specifically targeting the Ahmakiq Undae region. This region, located in Titan's equatorial zone, is characterized by vast fields of dunes composed primarily of hydrocarbons, which are organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen. The mission aims to study the complex chemistry and potential for prebiotic processes on Titan, which has a thick atmosphere rich in nitrogen and methane. Dragonfly, a rotorcraft lander, will be capable of flying between multiple sites on Titan, allowing for extensive exploration of diverse geological features. The mission will investigate the moon's surface composition, atmospheric conditions, and potential for habitability, providing insights into the processes that may have led to the emergence of life on Earth. item.title: White House Video Shows Press Ban Backfiring as Coverage Issues Arise
item.description: The White House press pool has suspended coverage of daily events following the ban of CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from the White House grounds. This decision led to awkward moments during a Monday ribbon-cutting ceremony on the South Lawn, where audio from the event was completely inaudible due to the absence of professional press coverage. The president's remarks were drowned out by the sound of Marine One, the presidential helicopter, which was operating nearby. The lack of professional audio equipment and coverage became evident when the White House's social media accounts attempted to broadcast the event, resulting in a video with no clear audio. Newsmax, a right-wing network, acknowledged that Trump's press ban was 'backfiring just a little bit.' The White House defended its decision, stating that access changes were 'nothing new' and that the rule was 'always our side stays in.' item.title: 2028 Presidential Hopefuls Stake Out Positions on Artificial Intelligence Regulation
item.description:
The debate over artificial intelligence is becoming a defining issue in the early stages of the 2028 presidential race, with prospective candidates from both parties scrambling to articulate their positions amid rising public concern about the technology's risks. Democratic hopefuls, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, and Senators Mark Kelly and Cory Booker, have recently pushed for stronger federal safeguards, third-party oversight of advanced AI systems, and support for workers displaced by automation. Newsom signed an executive order accelerating implementation of state laws requiring independent safety evaluations of AI systems, while also convening experts to strengthen California's AI safety regime. He advocates for mandatory 'kill switches' to shut down rogue systems but stops short of calling for a development pause.

item.title: Shooting at South Los Angeles Senior Living Facility Leaves Three Injured, One Critical
item.description: A gunman entered a senior living facility in South Los Angeles on Monday morning, opening fire and wounding three staff members, one of whom was in critical condition. The incident occurred before 11 a.m. near West 70th Street and Denver Avenue. The shooter, who was a worker at the facility, shot three employees inside the lobby before moving further into the building. Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) officers responded within two minutes, finding three victims in the lobby. They later located the gunman on another floor and took him into custody. The suspect was described as a man in his 60s. The victims included a woman in her 40s, a woman in her 60s, and a man in his 60s, all of whom were transported to a local hospital. One victim was reported to be in critical condition, though it was not immediately clear which individual was in critical condition. item.title: Reform UK Wales elects Helen Jenner as new leader after narrow victory over rival
item.description: The Guardian reports on the leadership change within Reform UK in Wales, where Helen Jenner has been elected as the new leader following a close contest with Jason O'Connell. The vote resulted in Jenner securing 17 votes to O'Connell's 15, marking a narrow victory. Multiple sources within Reform UK indicate concerns about potential future leadership challenges, with fears that another leadership contest may arise within six months. The article also covers broader political developments, including the appointment of Professor Peter Fonagy to investigate mental health conditions, ADHD, and autism, who challenges the claims made by figures like Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage that young people are part of a 'snowflake generation.' Fonagy argues that young people are facing genuine mental health challenges and that adults have failed to provide adequate support. item.title: UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese Faces U.S. Sanctions Amid International Law Crisis
item.description: The article discusses the sanctions imposed by the Trump administration on Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territories occupied since 1967. Albanese has been vocal in her criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank, documenting war crimes and genocide through detailed reports. Her office has identified 48 companies and institutions, including major tech firms like Microsoft, Google, and Lockheed Martin, that profit from the occupation and genocide of Palestinians. The sanctions, announced on July 10, 2025, are part of a broader effort to silence her and undermine international legal mechanisms. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned her support for the International Criminal Court (ICC), which had issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. item.title: Former GOP Operative Criticizes MAGA Movement Following Trump's Media Ban
item.description: On September 21, 2026, a former Republican operative, Rick Wilson, founder of the anti-Trump group The Lincoln Project, publicly criticized the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement on social media after President Donald Trump banned major media outlets including CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds. Trump's decision, which he justified by claiming these outlets spread 'fake news,' has already led to significant backlash, as major networks like Fox News, ABC News, CBS News, and NBC News withdrew from the White House press pool in protest, resulting in a silent broadcast during a helipad unveiling ceremony. Wilson's post on X questioned the hypocrisy of MAGA supporters, asking, 'So when the next Democratic Administration bans Fox, Newsmax, and OAN from the White House, you'll be fine, right, MAGA? item.title: White House Announces 'Trump TV' as Media Restrictions Intensify
item.description: The White House has sparked controversy with a series of social media posts promoting a new initiative called 'Trump TV,' which has drawn immediate criticism from media professionals and political commentators. The administration began teasing the platform on Monday, just hours after major television networks ceased providing shared video coverage of President Donald Trump. The White House posted a six-second video showing an old television flickering with static before displaying Trump's face, followed by a second teaser featuring a satellite news truck driving past the White House. In a third post, the administration announced, 'Streaming 24/7. Live at 7 p.m. Trump TV,' without providing further details. This announcement comes amid heightened tensions between the Trump administration and major media outlets. item.title: Survival Economy in Gaza: How Humanitarian Aid and Black Markets Shape Daily Life Amid Genocide
item.description: The article details the collapse of Gaza's traditional economy under the ongoing Israeli military operations, which have been described as genocide. Shaimaa Eid, a Gaza-based journalist, provides a firsthand account of how the humanitarian system has deteriorated since the UNRWA (United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees) was sidelined. Initially, UNRWA served as the primary distributor of food aid, but after its funding was suspended and its role marginalized, the U.S.- and Israel-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) took over. This shift has led to a chaotic distribution system where food points, often targeted by Israeli forces, have become dangerous 'death traps.' Civilians face violence while trying to access aid, and local armed groups control much of the food supply, turning distribution into a system based on money, connections, or survival rather than need. item.title: Former Biden Official Criticizes GOP Pundit for Comparing Trump's Media Restrictions to Biden's Practices
item.description: Former Biden White House communications director Kate Bedingfield confronted former Republican Representative Patrick McHenry on CNN's 'The Arena' regarding his comparison of President Donald Trump's media restrictions to President Joe Biden's communication practices. During the segment, McHenry argued that Trump's frequent media access, including Oval Office briefings three or four times a week, outweighed Biden's approach, which he claimed involved fewer daily interactions with reporters. Bedingfield rejected the comparison, stating that Biden's daily pool coverage was 'substantively very different' from Trump's targeted media ban on CNN, MSN, and Politico. She emphasized that equating the two scenarios was 'ludicrous and a little dangerous,' noting that Biden's strategy involved open, daily interactions with the press, while Trump's actions restricted specific outlets from covering his administration. item.title: Iran's Revolution and Its Complex Legacy: A Nation of Contradictions
item.description: The article discusses the 1979 Iranian Revolution and its aftermath, highlighting the complex political and social dynamics that have shaped modern Iran. It begins by examining the intellectual influences on key figures like Ali Shariati, who combined Islamic theology with liberation movements against oppression, feudalism, capitalism, and imperialism. The revolution, led by figures such as Ayatollah Khomeini, initially united a broad spectrum of society but soon faced internal divisions and violence, including the execution of thousands of political opponents. The article notes that Iran's political system, a unique blend of clerical governance and democratic institutions, has shown more institutional dynamism than the U.S. political system, with alternating conservative and reformist governments. item.title: ICE removes 16,000 detainees with final deportation orders from public database, causing family distress
item.description: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has quietly removed thousands of detainees with final deportation orders from its public locator database, making it nearly impossible for families and attorneys to locate their loved ones. According to The New Republic, the agency implemented this change on September 15 without public announcement, a move confirmed by three current and former agency officials. Immigration attorneys reported sudden difficulties in locating clients in the system, prompting the American Immigration Lawyers Association to alert its members. Data from the Deportation Data Project, a collaboration between UCLA and UC Berkeley, shows that approximately 16,000 people were processed into ICE detention with final removal orders in July alone, representing over a third of all individuals detained that month. item.title: Popular Mechanics Reviews Top Smart Glasses with AI and Camera Features for 2026
item.description: Popular Mechanics has tested and reviewed the best smart glasses for 2026, focusing on devices that integrate artificial intelligence and camera capabilities. The article highlights five top models: the Ray-Ban Meta Scriber Optics Gen 2 as the best overall, Meta Glasses Adventurer as the best value, Even Realities Even G2 for productivity, Meta Oakley HSTN for outdoor use, and Rokid A.I. Glasses for POV footage. The review emphasizes that smart glasses have evolved beyond simple wearables, now offering camera functionality, AI assistants, and open-ear audio. The author notes that while these devices can enhance daily life by reducing phone dependency, they also raise privacy concerns, particularly regarding discreet camera use. item.title: Exploring East London's River Lea: A Convergence of Nature, History, and Urban Life
item.description: The River Lea, once a vital industrial waterway in East London, has transformed into a vibrant green space where nature, urban history, and unconventional living coexist. Photographer Mattia Corato documents this evolving landscape through his series 'Along the River Lea,' capturing the interplay between wild nature and human presence along the riverbanks. Corato, who moved to Clapton a few years ago, began cycling along the waterways and discovered a deeply urban yet natural environment filled with human traces and overgrown spaces. The river, historically crucial for transporting coal and raw materials during the Industrial Revolution, now serves as a recreational area, creating an unexpected green oasis in the heart of the city. The communities living along the riverbanks reflect the area's modern identity, with some drawn to the freedom of water-based living and others seeking affordable housing as property costs rise. item.title: Adapting Pomodoro Technique to Engineering Workflows: Balancing Focus and Interruptions
item.description: The article discusses how engineers can adapt the Pomodoro technique to fit their specific work patterns, rather than using the standard 25-minute intervals. It explains that the original Pomodoro method was designed for paper-based clerical tasks with frequent hand-offs, but modern engineering work involves longer, more complex tasks like debugging, code reviews, and compiler rebuilds. The author argues that forcing a 25-minute break during these tasks can disrupt workflow and reduce productivity. Instead, the article provides a method for determining the optimal Pomodoro cycle length based on an engineer's actual work patterns. This involves logging focus spans over several days and categorizing them into quick switches (under 15 minutes), standard spans (15-45 minutes), deep spans (45-90 minutes), and marathon spans (90+ minutes). The article then explains how to calculate the ideal block length based on three factors: target sustained focus per block, realistic interruption budget

item.title: Carnival Cruise Line Passenger Missing After Overboard Incident Captured on Camera
item.description: A passenger on a Carnival Cruise Line ship returning to Long Beach from Mexico went overboard over the weekend and is still missing. The U.S. Coast Guard confirmed on Monday that it was actively searching for a 56-year-old man. Video footage captured by passengers and shared on social media shows a Carnival staff member announcing to guests that a passenger had gone overboard. The announcement stated, 'Folks, our team have completed a review of our man overboard cameras, and sadly, sadly, we have been able to confirm the guest has gone overboard,' according to the video. The passenger's family and companions were notified, and local authorities continued the search. Carnival Cruise Line confirmed the incident in a statement, noting that when notified of a missing guest, the ship's team initiated search procedures, including reviewing CCTV footage and notifying both the U.S. and Mexico Coast Guards. The company also stated it was providing support to the family traveling with the guest.

item.title: ESA Confirms Ariane 6 Launch Schedule Adjustments Due to Engine Turbopump Anomaly
item.description: The European Space Agency (ESA) has confirmed delays in the Ariane 6 launch schedule following reports of an engine turbopump anomaly. French news outlet La Tribune first reported an issue with an unspecified Ariane 6 component on September 17, 2026, with additional checks expected to disrupt Arianespace's planned launch cadence for the remainder of 2026. The following day, Peter de Selding's Space Intel Report identified the component as an engine turbopump, with the anomaly discovered during ground evaluations in August. This issue could result in only one or two additional Ariane 6 launches in 2026, rather than the previously planned three or four missions. ESA, responsible for the overall management of the Ariane 6 program, acknowledged the delays but declined to comment on the root cause. item.title: Behind the Scenes: Bill Murray’s Improvised Performance in Caddyshack
item.description:
The article looks back at Bill Murray’s work as groundskeeper Carl Spackler in Caddyshack (1980), focusing on the improvisational approach that helped make the character one of the film’s most memorable. Murray was originally expected to have only a small role, and his availability was limited because he was working on Saturday Night Live. He spent about six days filming in Florida, during which director Harold Ramis created opportunities for him to improvise and expand the character.
Several of Carl Spackler’s best-known moments were developed largely through improvisation. The famous “Cinderella story” sequence, in which Carl imagines himself winning the Masters while cutting flowers with a grass whip, was based on only a brief description of the action rather than a fully written speech. Murray also improvised Carl’s elaborate story about caddying for the Dalai Lama. These scenes became central examples of the loose, spontaneous style that characterized much of Murray’s performance

item.title: EU and US Reach Preliminary Trade Deal with 15% Tariffs on European Exports
item.description: The European Union and the United States have reached a preliminary trade agreement following negotiations between President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Scotland. Under the deal, the US will impose a 15% tariff on all EU products, which is half the 30% tariff Trump had threatened to implement starting Friday. The agreement also includes provisions for the EU to open its markets to US exporters with 0% tariffs on certain products. Von der Leyen praised the deal, stating it would bring stability to both allies, which together represent nearly a third of global trade. Trump claimed the EU would increase its investment in the US by $600 billion, including US military equipment, and spend $750 billion on US energy sources over the next three years. This investment is expected to reduce Europe's dependence on Russian energy. Some products, such as aircraft, aircraft parts, certain chemicals, and agricultural goods, will be exempt from tariffs. item.title: Book Publishers Forge Partnerships and Licensing Deals with AI Companies
item.description: Book publishers are increasingly engaging with the AI industry through partnerships, licensing agreements, and internal AI tool development. According to Publisher's Weekly, there are at least 15 author-driven lawsuits against AI companies, while publishers have filed around 10 coordinated lawsuits of their own. Despite these legal challenges, some publishers are building bridges with AI companies. Google recently partnered with major publishers including Bloomsbury, De Gruyter Brill, Johns Hopkins University Press, Macmillan, O'Reilly Media, and Penguin Random House to enhance e-books on Google Play with AI features, allowing readers to interact with book content, ask questions, and generate tools like quizzes and slideshows. HarperCollins became the first of the Big Five publishers to publicly disclose an AI licensing deal in 2024, earning $5,000 per title annually, split equally between the publisher and authors. item.title: Trump's Ribbon-Cutting Event Lacks Audio After White House Bans News Outlets
item.description:
President Donald Trump's ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new White House helipad on Monday, September 21, 2026, was marred by technical issues as the audio feed was completely garbled, leaving journalists unable to hear his remarks. The White House announced the event on X, providing only its own live video feed, while traditional television networks that typically cover presidential events had suspended coverage earlier that day. Media reports indicated that the audio was 'completely garbled,' with multiple journalists noting they could not hear Trump speaking through the White House stream. Politico's Sophia Cai described the situation as 'nothing but static for 9 minutes,' while New York Times media reporter Michael M. Grynbaum confirmed the audio was 'completely garbled and we are unable to hear the president's remarks.'

item.title: The Two-State Solution is Dead: A Reality Check on Palestinian Statehood
item.description: The article argues that the two-state solution for Israel and Palestine is no longer viable, having been declared 'dead' by geography, justice, and reality. The author, Hala Jaber, states that the concept of a two-state solution has become an empty promise, a diplomatic illusion that distracts from the realities of occupation and apartheid. Israeli leaders, including Netanyahu, have explicitly stated they have no intention of allowing a sovereign Palestinian state, with Netanyahu declaring in July 2025 that any independent Palestinian state would pose a threat to Israel's existence. The article details how the current situation makes a Palestinian state impossible: the proposed territories (Gaza and West Bank) are disconnected, with Israel controlling all borders, airspace, and movement between them. item.title: Best iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Cases: Top Picks Tested by CNN Editors
item.description:
CNN Underscored's editors have tested iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max cases from leading brands including Apple, OtterBox, and Casetify to identify the best protective options for Apple's latest flagship smartphones. The article provides a comprehensive roundup of 11 top-performing cases that offer varying levels of protection, style, and functionality to suit different user preferences and needs.
The testing process involved hands-on evaluation of cases from multiple manufacturers, assessing factors such as drop protection ratings, material quality, MagSafe compatibility, button responsiveness, and overall design aesthetics. Editors looked for cases that could adequately protect the expensive devices while maintaining usability and not adding excessive bulk.

item.title: Study Reveals Unilateral Sanctions Cause Half a Million Civilian Deaths Annually
item.description: A study published in The Lancet, a leading medical journal, reveals that unilateral sanctions, primarily imposed by the United States, cause approximately half a million civilian deaths each year. The research, conducted by Francisco Rodríguez, Silvio Rendón, and Mark Weisbrot, analyzed the impact of international sanctions from 1971 to 2021. The study found that sanctions have led to 564,258 annual deaths, surpassing the number of deaths from combat (106,000 annually) and approaching the total death toll from wars, including civilian casualties. The most vulnerable groups affected are children under five years old, who accounted for 51% of all deaths caused by sanctions during the study period. The research highlights that U.S. and European Union sanctions are more lethal than those imposed by the United Nations, largely due to the global dominance of the U.S. dollar and euro in international transactions, as well as the extraterritorial application of U.S. sanctions. item.title: Meta's AI Assistant Muse Blocked by Amazon from Shopping on Its Platform
item.description: Meta's AI assistant, Muse, has been blocked from using Amazon.com, according to a recent report by TechCrunch. Users of Muse began encountering an error message when attempting to purchase goods on Amazon, stating, 'Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.' This indicates that Amazon has explicitly prohibited the use of Meta's AI agent for shopping purposes. The block appears to be part of a broader tension between tech giants, as Amazon has its own foundation models and inference platforms. Amazon may be hesitant to allow third-party AI agents like Muse to handle transactions due to potential liability issues. If Muse makes an incorrect order, Amazon would be responsible for resolving customer complaints and vendor disputes. item.title: Lunar Settlements Face Water Scarcity Challenges, Study Reveals
item.description: A recent study published in the journal Frontiers in Space Technologies has revealed that large-scale human settlements on the moon would face significant challenges due to insufficient water resources. According to researchers led by Martin Elvis, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a city of 1 million people would deplete the moon's estimated water supply in just 2.5 years without recycling. Even with a 98% water recycling rate, similar to that achieved on the International Space Station, such a city would only last 100 years, which researchers consider insufficient for sustainable long-term settlement. The study calculated that a smaller city of 100,000 people could sustain itself for 1,000 years, while a town of 10,000 people would have water resources lasting 10,000 years. item.title: German Liberals' Missteps on East German Identity in Recent Elections
item.description: The article discusses the author's reflections as a former editor-in-chief of Berliner Zeitung on the missteps of German liberals regarding the identity of East Germans. The author, Tomasz Kurianowicz, notes that German liberals have learned to take everyone's identity seriously except that of East Germans. This perspective is contextualized by recent election results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won approximately 38 percent of the vote, more than double its previous share. In Berlin, the Left party, which descends from East Germany's former ruling Communist Party, emerged as the strongest party citywide, while the AfD also made significant gains. In Berlin's eastern borough of Marzahn-Hellersdorf, the AfD was running above 30 percent in the borough assembly election. item.title: Opera Montana Premieres First-Ever Adaptation of 'A River Runs Through It'
item.description:
Opera Montana has made history with the world premiere of its operatic adaptation of Norman Maclean's beloved novella 'A River Runs Through It,' marking the first time the iconic Montana story has been transformed into an opera. The production debuted in Bozeman at the Ellen Theatre in September 2026, bringing a globally recognized piece of American literature to the stage in an entirely new form.
The opera features music by composer Zach Redler and a libretto by Kelley Rourke and Matt Foss. According to organizers, the production combines sweeping orchestral music with cinematic storytelling inspired by Montana's landscapes and waterways. To prepare for their roles, the cast even went fly-fishing on the Yellowstone River to authentically capture the story's deep connection to Montana's fishing culture.
Originally published in 1976, Maclean's semi-autobiographical novella follows brothers Norman and Paul Maclean as they navigate family expectations, faith, love, and personal struggle

item.title: Point Lepreau Nuclear Plant Shut Down Again Due to Heavy-Water Leak
item.description: The Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station in New Brunswick, Canada, has been shut down for the second time this month due to a heavy-water leak on an instrumentation line within the heat transport system. According to Joel Armstrong, the deputy site vice-president at Point Lepreau, the early indication systems detected the potential leak, allowing for a safe and predictable shutdown to facilitate repairs. The heavy-water system is critical for transferring heat from the reactor to conventional boilers filled with regular water, which then generates steam to power the plant turbines. Heavy water itself is not radioactive, but over time, when used in a reactor, it begins to produce tritium, a weak source of beta radiation that can increase cancer risk if consumed in extremely large quantities. item.title: Coinbase Opens IPO Market to US Retail Investors Through New Platform Feature
item.description:
Coinbase has announced a major expansion of its platform that will allow eligible retail investors in the United States to participate in initial public offerings (IPOs) for the first time. Starting with Oura's IPO this week, qualified Coinbase customers can request share allocations directly through the Coinbase app at the offer price before stocks begin trading on public exchanges.
The new feature works through Coinbase Capital Markets (CCM), a FINRA-registered broker-dealer that serves as a selling-group member in IPOs. Customers can navigate to a dedicated IPOs page in the app, select an active deal, fund their account, and submit a 'Conditional Offer to Buy' once the expected price range is announced. After the order book closes, shares are allocated using an established methodology and booked directly into customer accounts at the IPO price.

item.description:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art has helped develop an arrangement under which three centuries-old African masterworks owned by philanthropist and art collector Ceil Pulitzer will become part of Nigeria’s national collection. According to the information reported by the museum and The New York Times, there is no evidence that the works were stolen or illegally brought into the United States.
Nevertheless, the Met determined that the available documentation did not meet the standards required for the museum to add the pieces to its permanent collection. item.title: Newly Discovered 728-Foot Lunar Crater Highlights Impact Risks for Future Moon Bases
item.description:
Scientists have identified the largest newly formed impact crater ever observed in the solar system: a 728-foot-wide (222-meter) basin on the Moon officially named McGetchin crater. The crater appeared between April and May 2024 when a building-sized asteroid or comet fragment struck the lunar surface at high speed, releasing energy equivalent to roughly 15,500 tons of TNT. The discovery, detailed in two studies published in the journal Science Advances on September 16, 2026, offers researchers an unprecedented, real-time view of the aftermath of a massive lunar impact and the extensive debris field it created.
The crater measures 728 feet across and reaches a depth of 141 feet (43 meters), making it more than twice the length of an American football field and large enough to hold three vertically stacked school buses. Disturbances to the lunar dust were detected more than 62 miles (100 kilometers) from the impact site, underscoring how far-reaching the effects of such events can be.

While Google and Apple Maps quickly updated to reflect the new name for U.S. users, the reaction along Lake Ontario has been overwhelmingly negative, even among Trump supporters. item.description: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its Wide Field Instrument, a 300-megapixel infrared camera designed to capture vast areas of the cosmos with unprecedented detail. The instrument, which covers an area of sky larger than a full moon in a single image, will enable the telescope to conduct extensive surveys of the universe, providing valuable data for studying exoplanets, dark energy, and the distribution of matter. The activation process involved a meticulous cooling procedure, with the camera's detectors reaching temperatures as low as -225 degrees Fahrenheit (-143 degrees Celsius) before being powered on. Following the successful activation, engineers tested the camera's filters, focusing mechanisms, and calibration systems. The Coronagraph Instrument, designed to directly image exoplanets by blocking starlight, also completed its initial checkout, confirming that all systems are functioning as expected.
