item.title: Rare 1887 Photograph Reveals New York City's Short Tail Gang in Historic Underwater Setting
item.description: The article discusses a rare photograph captured in 1887 by photographer Jacob Riis, depicting members of the Short Tail Gang gathered under a pier at Corlears Hook in New York City. The photograph, taken in 1889, is the only known image of this notorious gang from the 1880s-1890s. The Short Tail Gang, also known as the Short Tails, was an Irish gang active in the Corlear's Hook section of the Lower East Side in Manhattan. Their distinctive short-tailed jackets gave the gang its name and served as a makeshift uniform in the harsh conditions of tenement life and street survival. The gang operated in the vicinity of Rivington Street, near Mangin and Goerck Streets, and worked the New York City waterfront, plundering ships of their cargo on the East River. They were one of the few 19th-century New York gangs that allowed their members to be photographed, which was unusual as most criminal photographs from that era were police mug shots taken in fear of identification and arrest. item.title: Underground Experiment Challenges Gravity's Role in Quantum Decoherence
item.description: A deep-underground experiment conducted at Italy's Gran Sasso National Laboratory has challenged a long-standing theory about why quantum mechanics appears to disappear in the macroscopic world. The research, published in the New Journal of Physics in June 2026, tested a model proposed by Hungarian physicist Frigyes Károlyházy in the 1960s, which suggested that tiny fluctuations in spacetime caused by gravity gradually destroy quantum superpositions. The experiment involved searching for extremely faint electromagnetic radiation that would be emitted if such spacetime fluctuations existed, using a highly shielded germanium detector. After 62 days of measurements, researchers found no evidence of the predicted radiation signal. This absence of a signal rules out one prominent explanation for quantum decoherence, which is the process by which quantum effects like superposition disappear as objects become larger. item.title: Ancient Anglo-Saxon Remains Unearthed During Home Renovation in Kent, England
item.description: In 2019, a routine home renovation project in Wye, Kent, England, unexpectedly uncovered ancient human remains, causing a temporary police investigation. Ross Sledger, the homeowner, initially believed the bones belonged to a farm animal or pet when a builder discovered them during a kitchen addition. Upon learning the remains were human, Sledger expressed shock, stating, 'You must be joking, this is a wind-up,' but the builder confirmed the seriousness of the find. Archaeologists later determined the bones were Anglo-Saxon, dating back approximately 1,000 years. The discovery included a femur, two skulls, ribs, part of a pelvis, and fragments of a humerus and finger bones. Police treated the site as a potential crime scene, with officers stationed overnight and neighbors' floodlights and a barking dog disrupting Sledger's sleep. item.title: Insomniac Games clarifies restroom sign issue in Marvel's Wolverine as UV map bug, denies AI use
item.description: Insomniac Games, the developer behind Marvel's Wolverine, has denied using generative AI in the game after fans noticed an unusual restroom sign in the game's environment. Community director James Stevenson addressed the concern on social media, stating that the sign was not AI-generated but rather the result of a 'UV map bug' that affected the symbol's appearance. Stevenson clarified on X/Twitter that the issue would be fixed in an upcoming update, emphasizing that 'there are no AI generated assets in Marvel's Wolverine.' The controversy arose when players shared screenshots of the sign, which appeared distorted and unusual, prompting speculation about AI involvement. Stevenson's response included a detailed explanation of the technical issue, noting that the bug occurred during the UV mapping process, a standard technique in 3D modeling where textures are applied to surfaces. item.title: Hollywood Executives Collaborate with Israel to Defend War Crimes, Leaked Emails Reveal
item.description: The leaked Sony Files, published by WikiLeaks, reveal that prominent Hollywood producers and entertainment executives have been collaborating with the Israeli government to defend its military actions in Gaza, particularly during the 2014 Operation Protective Edge. The emails show a coordinated effort to shape public opinion, silence critics, and counter the BDS (Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions) movement. Key figures such as Glenn D. Feig, Ron Rotholz, and Ryan Kavanaugh discussed strategies to repeat Israel's narrative 'ad infinitum' until it was accepted, with the goal of preventing Hollywood stars like Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem from labeling Israel's actions as 'genocide.' The emails also detail attempts to pressure institutions like the Cannes Film Festival and the Metropolitan Opera to cancel events or performances that criticized Israel, such as the opera 'The Death of Klinghoffer.' item.title: Apartment Landlords Face Looming Debt Crisis as Interest Rates Rise Under Trump Administration
item.description: The Wall Street Journal has highlighted a significant crisis in the U.S. apartment rental market that threatens to destabilize the economy under President Donald Trump. According to the Journal, big money apartment landlords are confronting a looming debt crisis, with over $1.8 trillion in mortgage payments due within the next decade, including $757 billion by 2028. This debt burden is particularly acute for landlords who secured loans during 2020-2021 when interest rates were near 3%, as they now face refinance rates nearly double that amount. The situation has been exacerbated by a construction boom in Sunbelt cities like Phoenix, Denver, Atlanta, and Austin, which flooded the market with luxury units that remain unfilled. This has led to landlords selling properties at a loss, returning keys to lenders, or struggling to cover increased mortgage payments, reminiscent of the 2008 housing crisis. item.title: Deep-sea fish observed walking backwards for first time, study reveals
item.description: A groundbreaking study has documented the first-ever footage of a deep-sea fish walking backwards, a behavior previously unrecorded in fish species. Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University and the Southern Marine Science and Engineering Guangdong Laboratory observed three species of armored searobin (Scalicus engyceros, Paraheminodus murrayi, and Peristedion liorhynchus) in their natural habitat in the northern South China Sea using remotely operated and human-occupied vehicles. The armored searobin, commonly referred to as a 'fish-prawn hybrid' due to its unique appearance combining fish-like body with shrimp-like appendages, was filmed using specialized rays extending from its pectoral fins to move along the seafloor. The footage confirmed that these fish can walk not only forwards and sideways but also backwards using their free pectoral-fin rays. item.title: Accenture Stock Rises 6% on $1 Billion AI Safety Partnership with Anthropic
item.description:
Accenture's stock jumped 6% in premarket trading Monday after the company announced a major AI safety partnership with Anthropic, the artificial intelligence firm behind the Claude chatbot. Under the deal, Accenture will embed a team of assessors inside Anthropic to rigorously evaluate its AI models, a move both companies describe as a significant step toward advancing AI technology responsibly.
The partnership will be led by Faculty, a U.K.-based AI company that Accenture acquired earlier this year. Both Accenture and Anthropic plan to commit approximately $1 billion each over the next five years to fund AI safety initiatives. While details remain limited, the collaboration builds on previous work between the two companies to integrate AI technologies into client operations.
The announcement comes at a critical time for Accenture, whose shares have fallen roughly 30% this year amid investor concerns about corporate IT spending and fears that AI solutions could reduce demand for trad

item.title: Democrats worry Republican spending advantage could limit their gains in the 2026 midterms
item.description:
Democratic leaders and campaign operatives are privately warning that the party lacks enough money to take full advantage of what they view as a favorable political environment in the 2026 midterm elections. Republican campaigns and conservative super PACs have sharply increased spending in competitive House and Senate races, leaving Democrats concerned that they may be unable to defend vulnerable incumbents, respond to negative advertising, or compete in newly targeted districts.
According to AdImpact figures cited in the article, Republicans have reserved approximately $682 million in advertising for House and Senate races between now and Election Day, compared with about $491 million reserved by Democrats. The gap is especially significant in several battlegrounds, including Texas, Iowa, New Hampshire, Alaska, and North Carolina. In New Hampshire, for example, Republicans have booked roughly $24 million in advertising, while Democrats have reserved about $15 million.

item.title: Fall Color Palette Quiz Reveals Personal Style Through Seasonal Questions
item.description: The article introduces a personality quiz created by BuzzFeed staff member Sydney Mills, designed to match readers with an autumn color palette based on their answers to specific fall-themed questions. The quiz, titled 'Answer These Oddly Specific Fall Questions And I'll Give You An Autumnal Color Palette,' invites users to engage with questions about seasonal preferences, such as opinions on soup, flea market finds, and early darkness in autumn. The content emphasizes that fall is not just a season but a cultural phenomenon that inspires strong opinions on various topics. The quiz aims to provide a fun, interactive experience that connects personal tastes with seasonal aesthetics. The article also includes promotional elements for BuzzFeed's quiz platform, encouraging users to create their own quizzes or join the community. It highlights the popularity of quizzes as a form of entertainment and self-expression, particularly during the fall season. The piece is structured as a standard

item.title: Trump and Mamdani to Meet in New York City on Monday
item.description: President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani are scheduled to meet in person at Gracie Mansion, the mayor's official residence in Manhattan, on Monday, according to the mayor's office and the White House. This will be their third meeting to date, with the focus of the discussion centered on issues affecting New York City and its residents. The White House and the mayor's press office have confirmed the meeting details, emphasizing that the discussions will address matters pertinent to New Yorkers. The meeting is set to take place at 7:55 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2026, as reported by The Washington Post. The location, Gracie Mansion, is a historic site that has served as the official residence of New York City mayors since 1942. The meeting comes amid ongoing discussions between federal and city officials regarding various policy matters, including public safety, infrastructure, and economic development. item.title: Optometrist Advises Varied Colorful Diet for Eye Health Beyond Five Daily Servings
item.description: During National Eye Health Week, optometrist Francesca Marchetti emphasizes the importance of a varied diet rich in colorful fruits and vegetables for maintaining healthy eyes. According to research by MacuShield, only 25% of Britons believe their diet provides all necessary nutrients for good vision, while 32% would cut fresh produce first during a cost-of-living crisis. Marchetti recommends consuming a wide variety of colorful foods, including leafy greens, red peppers, and berries, to ensure intake of essential nutrients like lutein, zeaxanthin, and vitamin C. She also suggests eating more than five servings of fruits and vegetables daily. The article highlights five budget-friendly foods beneficial for eye health: frozen spinach (rich in lutein), tinned sardines (high in omega-3 fatty acids), tinned sweetcorn (contains zeaxanthin), eggs (source of vitamin B2), and tinned beans (rich in zinc). item.title: Democrats Show Optimism in Gerrymandered Republican Districts Amid Internal Polls
item.description: The article discusses growing optimism among Democrats regarding the 2026 midterm elections, particularly in traditionally Republican (deep-red) districts that have been gerrymandered. According to a discussion on CNN News Central featuring Andrew Desiderio and Leigh Ann Caldwell, Democrats are increasingly confident about their prospects in several competitive districts, including Alabama's 1st congressional district (represented by Shomari Figures) and Florida's 9th district (represented by Congressman Darren Soto). These districts are described as 'Trump plus-14' or 'Trump plus-18' areas, meaning they have historically favored Republican candidates by significant margins. Despite the gerrymandered nature of these districts, internal polls suggest Democrats may have a stronger position than previously anticipated. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) is reportedly investing resources in Alabama's district, indicating some level of confidence in potentially flipping

item.title: Ukraine's Nuclear Disarmament and the Budapest Memorandum: A Historical Perspective on Western Policy
item.description: The article examines the Budapest Memorandum of 1994, which guaranteed Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity in exchange for its nuclear disarmament. It argues that Western powers, particularly NATO and its member states, have violated the memorandum's spirit long before Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea and 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The author, György Varga, a former Hungarian ambassador, highlights that Ukraine had declared itself a neutral, non-aligned state in 1990, reaffirmed in 1991 and 1996, with its constitution explicitly stating neutrality. Despite this, NATO's 2008 decision to include Ukraine as a future member, supported by Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, violated Ukraine's sovereignty and its declared neutrality. The article further details how Western powers, including the EU and NATO, supported the 2014 coup that ousted President Viktor Yanukovych, which led to the conflict in eastern Ukraine and Crimea's secession.

item.title: Patrick Clancy discusses forgiveness and grief after children's deaths in first televised interview
item.description:
Patrick Clancy, the former husband of Lindsay Clancy, has spoken publicly for the first time on television since a jury failed to reach a verdict in her murder trial. In an interview with CBS News' “60 Minutes,” he discussed the deaths of their three children, his grief, his decision to forgive Lindsay, and the continuing legal and public controversy surrounding the case.
The children, Cora, Dawson and eight-month-old Callan, were strangled in the family's Massachusetts home on January 24, 2023. Callan survived the initial attack but died four days later in Patrick's arms. During the interview, Patrick recalled writing tributes to his other children while holding Callan and explained that he chose to forgive Lindsay because he believed severe mental illness contributed to what happened. He said he feared that failing to forgive her would leave him consumed by anger.

item.title: Converse removes K-pop ad and apologizes after backlash over imagery resembling KKK hoods
item.description:
Converse, the American footwear brand owned by Nike, has issued a public apology and removed an advertisement after widespread criticism that the image evoked racist symbolism associated with the Ku Klux Klan. The ad, which appeared on Instagram, featured K-pop star Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers. Critics pointed out that the lighting on her skirt created a white triangular shape resembling a KKK hood, while the way she held the shoes made them appear similar to the dangling feet of a lynching victim.
In a statement released on Friday, Converse acknowledged the harm caused by the image. 'We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong,' the company said. The brand confirmed it had removed the ad from its official channels and was working to delete it from all platforms where it had appeared. item.title: El crepúsculo de la normalidad. De la hipótesis del colapso a la era de las convulsiones ecopolíticas – LOS NIÑOS PERDIDOS blog de Emilio Santiago Muíño
item.description: The article "El crepúsculo de la normalidad. De la hipótesis del colapso a la era de las convulsiones ecopolíticas" by Emilio Santiago Muíño explores the intersection of ecological crisis, political shifts, and social inequality in the context of the 21st century. The author analyzes how the global response to climate change has been shaped by political ideologies, particularly focusing on the rise of right-wing populism and its impact on environmental policies. The piece references historical parallels, such as the comparison between contemporary climate denialism and the rise of fascism in the early 20th century, drawing on works by scholars like Carl Amery and Bruno Latour. The author argues that the current ecological crisis is not merely an environmental issue but a political one, deeply intertwined with economic structures and power dynamics. item.title: Eugenio Castro: A Surrealist Poet's Legacy in Madrid's Urban Landscape
item.description: The blog post 'En memoria de Eugenio Castro' by Emilio Santiago Muíño commemorates the passing of Eugenio Castro, a prominent figure in the Surrealist movement and a poet deeply connected to Madrid's urban landscape. Castro, who died on March 2, 2024, was known for his poetic works that reimagined Madrid through a surrealist lens, transforming ordinary city spaces into magical, symbolic realms. The post highlights Castro's unique perspective on the city, where he found profound meaning in seemingly mundane locations like streets, plazas, and old buildings. He believed that places such as the Gran Boscoso, the street Cabeza, and the Calle Tres Peces held deep, almost mystical significance, where 'the thought is unleashed' and 'the conjuration of dreams is reorganized.' Castro's writings, including 'H' and 'Madrid Rediviva,' explore how everyday urban spaces can become 'places-ágora' that bridge the gap between memory and reality, personal and collective experience. item.title: US Million Person Study on Low-Dose Radiation Exposure Yields Preliminary Findings Contradicting Presidential Views
item.description: The US Million Person Study on low dose rate exposures to radiation has released preliminary findings that directly challenge the current US President's stance on radiation risk assessment. This large-scale study, which examines health effects from prolonged low-level radiation exposure among approximately one million nuclear workers and military veterans, represents the most comprehensive research of its kind to date. The study's findings include associations between occupational radiation exposure and Parkinson's disease, low risk of lung cancer, increased risk of leukemia (excluding chronic lymphocytic leukemia), evidence of increased solid cancers, and detection of chromosomal damage 65 years after exposure to nuclear weapons testing fallout. These results align with previous studies like the INWORKS study of nuclear industry workers, which found radiation risks higher than the Life Span Study (LSS) but broadly similar to it. item.title: Insider Explains Trump's Reaction to 'Terrible Week' Amid Political and Economic Challenges
item.description: A Washington, D.C. insider provided insight into President Donald Trump's recent actions following what he described as a 'terrible week' for the administration. According to Jim VandeHei, co-founder of Axios, Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House was driven by mounting pressures across multiple fronts. VandeHei characterized the move as 'small, silly, and stupid,' noting it would not significantly impact media coverage and likely face legal challenges. He explained that Trump's frustration stemmed from a combination of factors including rising interest rates, judicial restraints on presidential actions, a Republican congresswoman's ad criticizing immigration policies, record-high gas and diesel prices, persistent inflation, low poll numbers, and a struggling Republican Party. item.description: Despite recent court victories blocking Trump administration efforts to interfere with California's election process, the state continues to face significant challenges from federal authorities. Los Angeles County's top election official, Dean Logan, confirmed that his office has received multiple federal grand jury subpoenas demanding voter registration information on dozens of individuals, which appear to be part of a nationwide Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizens allegedly voting illegally. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has claimed without evidence that over 190,000 noncitizens may be registered to vote in California, a claim state officials have called baseless. item.description: The article discusses a strategic vision for Russia's future, emphasizing a shift away from European influence and towards Siberia and Asian markets. The author, Sergei Karaganov, argues that Russia should complete its 'European journey' of over three centuries, which has brought both benefits and significant costs including constant wars and ideological conflicts. item.title: Trump's Corruption and Lies Threaten Democratic Trust, Analyst Warns
item.description: The article discusses the growing distrust in the U.S. government, particularly under President Donald Trump, citing a recent Economist/YouGov poll showing 53% of Americans describe Trump as 'corrupt' and 51% as 'dangerous.' Gallup's findings reveal 89% of Americans believe government corruption is widespread, the highest in two decades. The author, Thom Hartmann, draws parallels between current U.S. political issues and historical examples of democratic decline in countries like Colombia, Russia, and El Salvador. item.description: The article examines the evolving political landscape in Iran, arguing that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has become the true center of power within the Iranian regime, surpassing the influence of the clerical establishment and elected officials. The author, Erfan Fard, a counterterrorism analyst specializing in Iranian security structures, contends that Iran's political system has transformed from a Shiite theocracy into a militarized dictatorship where the IRGC, with its accumulated military, intelligence, and economic authority, now serves as the state's primary power center. The article notes that Iran's regime, which has long been characterized by ideological adventurism, corruption, and institutional decay, is now focused on survival rather than revolutionary expansion. item.description: Flock Safety, a surveillance technology company known for its license plate reader systems, has announced a voluntary employee separation program offering generous severance packages to staff as it faces significant customer attrition and growing privacy concerns. According to an internal email shared with WIRED, the company is providing a 'generous' severance package to employees who wish to leave, with applications opening on Friday and a deadline of October 2 for decisions. item.description: Democrats are exploring a strategy to impeach President Donald Trump's cabinet members as a way to hold the administration accountable, sidestepping the pitfalls that previously doomed their impeachment efforts against Trump. Thomas Massie (R-KY) introducing a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which reportedly caused House GOP leadership to send members home early for the campaign season to avoid a floor vote. item.title: GOP Congressman Faces Legal Threat Over Domestic Abuse Allegations in Campaign Ad
item.description: Representative Max Miller (R-OH), a Republican congressman from Ohio, is facing a legal challenge from his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter, over a campaign ad that highlights allegations of domestic abuse against Miller. The ad, which features a local sheriff recounting the accusations, claims that Miller has been accused of abuse by three women, including his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who is the daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno. According to the allegations, Miller threw hot water on his ex-wife, held a gun to her head, and broke their toddler daughter's collarbone. Miller's attorney, Alejandro Brito, who has also represented President Donald Trump, sent a cease-and-desist letter to WKYC, a Cleveland TV station, demanding they stop airing the ad, which he labeled as 'false, malicious, and defamatory.' item.description: The article discusses the author's lifelong struggle with sleep, detailing how poor sleep habits affected his childhood and adulthood. As a child, he would lie about going to bed early to avoid punishment from teachers, and as an adult, he engaged in behaviors like staying up late watching TV, drinking excessive cola, and using caffeine to stay awake. The author recounts a personal incident where he walked into a glass door while half-asleep at work, highlighting the dangers of sleep deprivation. He references a Nike report that emphasizes sleep's role in recovery, mood, immune function, and athletic performance, noting that regular exercise can improve sleep quality. item.description: The article by Rafael Poch de Feliu discusses a recent piece by Russian scholar Sergei Karagánov, which warns European leaders about the dangers of ignoring Russia's security concerns. Karagánov, a prominent Russian intellectual and former head of the Council for Foreign and Defense Policy, argues that Europe's current approach to Russia, particularly its support for Ukraine and military posturing, is dangerously escalatory. The article emphasizes that European leaders, including those in Berlin, London, and Paris, have renounced diplomacy and dialogue with Russia, instead pursuing a 'strategic defeat' of Russia through Ukraine. Karagánov's analysis highlights that Russia views Western actions as a threat to its sovereignty and security, and warns that if European nations send troops to Ukraine, they will be considered direct participants in the conflict, prompting Russian military responses. item.title: Cancer Research Malaysia Launches MeMoSA Platform to Enhance Oral Cancer Screening in Remote Areas
item.description: Cancer Research Malaysia has developed MeMoSA® (Mobile Mouth Screening Anywhere), a digital platform designed to bring oral cancer screening to underserved communities through a combination of telemedicine and artificial intelligence. The platform enables trained staff and volunteers to capture oral images using mobile devices, which are then reviewed remotely by dental specialists. MeMoSA® incorporates AI-supported image quality checks, underpinned by a dataset of over 30,000 clinically annotated oral mucosa images collected across five countries. This dataset, which includes lesion classifications and clinical diagnoses verified through biopsy or expert consensus, allows for the training of AI models to identify patterns associated with oral lesions. The platform functions as a screening support tool rather than a diagnostic system, aiming to identify individuals who may require further medical evaluation. item.title: Meta's Copyright System Used to Target Albanian Protesters Amid Political Unrest
item.description: Meta's copyright system is being exploited to suppress Albanian protesters, according to reports from WIRED. The 'Flamingo Revolution' protests, which have been ongoing for over three months in Albania's capital, Tirana, are demanding changes to laws allowing development on protected land and the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. The protests were initially sparked by a luxury resort project linked to Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner. In late August, a wave of Instagram account suspensions began, with protesters reporting copyright complaints against their posts. An NGO, Repro Uncensored, found evidence of coordinated 'brigading' attacks, where multiple copyright claims were filed against the same accounts in a short period. Martha Dimitratou, founder of Repro Uncensored, stated that nearly all affected accounts were targeted with copyright infringement reports, with some accounts receiving five to ten complaints within a short timeframe. item.title: Police officer injured in shooting outside Ontario synagogue during Yom Kippur services
item.description:
A police officer was shot outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, on Sunday evening as members of the local Jewish community gathered to observe Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. The incident occurred at approximately 7:10 p.m. near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue, located about 115 miles northeast of Toronto, according to the Belleville Police Service. Both the officer and the individual involved in the interaction sustained injuries and were transported to a hospital for treatment. Officials have not disclosed the officer's current condition but have stated that there is no ongoing threat to public safety.
The circumstances surrounding the shooting remain unclear, and investigators have not yet established a motive for the incident. Ontario Premier Doug Ford issued a statement praising the courage of the officer and first responders who acted quickly to protect the community. item.title: Trump Administration Proposes Conditional Funding Agreement with Top Universities
item.description: The Washington Post reports on a new strategy by the Trump administration targeting universities, which involves offering preferential federal funding to institutions that agree to adopt administration priorities. According to the article, last fall the Trump administration presented a 10-page compact to nine of the nation's top universities, proposing that they either sign the agreement to gain preferential access to federal funding or decline and risk losing those benefits. The article emphasizes that every college and university should agree on one fundamental principle: the U.S. government should never condition research funding on adherence to any administration's political agenda. The Hill, a nonpartisan publication covering government operations and politics-business intersections, authored the piece, highlighting concerns about government overreach into academic autonomy. item.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins the Toronto International Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award
item.description:
“La Bola Negra,” a Spanish-language film directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, won the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival. The audience-selected prize is closely watched during awards season because several past winners, including “Green Book” and “Nomadland,” later received major Oscar recognition.
The film follows three gay men whose stories unfold across several decades. It draws inspiration from an unfinished work by Federico García Lorca and features performances by singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz, and Glenn Close. The movie previously screened at the Cannes Film Festival, where Calvo and Ambrossi shared the Best Director award with Paweł Pawlikowski for “Fatherland.”

item.title: Trump Weighs U.S. Airstrikes Against Houthis After Saudi Arabia Appeals for Help
item.description:
President Donald Trump has repeatedly changed course over whether the United States should launch airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen after Saudi Arabia asked Washington for military assistance. The Iran-backed Houthis have renewed attacks against Saudi Arabia and seized strategically important areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
According to administration officials, Trump initially opposed striking the Houthis. After a conversation with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, however, he instructed the Pentagon to prepare for possible airstrikes. By Sunday, he had apparently postponed or canceled the operation, even though commanders had approved target lists and aircraft crews were preparing weapons. The White House did not publicly confirm the president's deliberations.

item.title: Trump Faces Critical Decision on Potential Nuclear Weapon Use in Iran Conflict
item.description: The article discusses the escalating tensions between the United States and Iran, focusing on President Trump's potential use of tactical nuclear weapons as a final act in what is described as a lost war. The author argues that Trump is trapped in a conflict that has already been lost, with the war lasting six months and failing to achieve regime change or popular uprising in Iran. Instead, the Iranian regime has hardened its leadership, and the U.S. military has been driven out of major bases across the region, with depleted missile stocks and an overstretched Navy. Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz and has recently gained control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, causing oil prices to rise above $110 per barrel and diesel prices to reach record levels. Trump's rhetoric has become increasingly delusional, dismissing the war as 'small potatoes' and suggesting the U.S. might stay in Iran to 'keep the oil like Venezuela.' item.title: Astrid Schiller: Iconic 1960s Fashion Model Captured in Rare Photographs
item.description: The article presents a collection of 35 vintage fashion portraits of Astrid Schiller, a prominent model during the 1960s. These images, captured by renowned photographers such as Helmut Newton, Richard Avedon, and F.C. Gundlach, showcase Schiller's elegance and sophisticated style throughout the decade. item.description: The iconic album cover for Motörhead's 1980 classic 'Ace of Spades' has been the subject of much curiosity regarding its actual filming location. The band members, including Lemmy, 'Fast' Eddie Clarke, and Phil 'Philthy Animal' Taylor, were photographed in a Western-themed setting with leather jackets, bullet belts, cowboy boots, and wide-brimmed hats. The photographer, Alan Ballard, was tasked with creating a bold, cinematic visual inspired by Western films and Clint Eastwood's 'Man with No Name' persona. The record company opted for a cost-effective location near London instead of traveling to the American Southwest. The sky was airbrushed to deepen blue tones and create the illusion of an arid desert landscape, making the overcast British sky appear as if it were a hot canyon. item.title: U.S. Authorities Seize Record-Breaking Martian Meteorite Amid Ownership Dispute
item.description:
A 54-pound meteorite from Mars, described by Sotheby’s as the largest Martian meteorite ever discovered, has become the focus of an international ownership dispute. The meteorite was reportedly found in Niger’s desert in 2023 and was auctioned by Sotheby’s in July 2025 for $5.3 million, making it the most expensive meteorite ever sold.
The sale attracted scrutiny after Nigerien authorities questioned whether the transaction violated a 1997 law protecting the country’s natural heritage. The government began investigating the meteorite’s origins and whether the auction house had failed to comply with national regulations. Sotheby’s subsequently paused the completion of the sale, according to Natasha Le Bel, a spokesperson for the auction house.

item.title: Chancellor Merz Vows to Continue Reforms Despite Historic Election Defeat in German States
item.description: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has faced a significant electoral setback in two state elections, including a historic defeat for his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. Projections from public broadcaster ARD indicate that the CDU received only 4.9% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the lowest result since World War II for the party in any state. The anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party made substantial gains, securing 37.9% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and 16.2% in Berlin. Despite these results, Merz rejected calls to retreat from his government's reform agenda, emphasizing that Germany's economic and political challenges necessitate difficult and potentially unpopular reforms. He stated, 'What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience,' and pledged to continue with reforms including tax cuts for low- and middle-income families, pension system overhauls, and bureaucratic reductions. item.description:
Israeli officials have expressed strong criticism and anger over an award-winning documentary titled 'NAZA,' which alleges that the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) used AI-assisted systems to identify targets for attacks in Gaza, often disregarding civilian casualties. The film, directed by Yuv al Abraham and Rachel Szor, received a 25-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival and won the Special Jury Prize. It is based on accounts from anonymous Israeli military and intelligence insiders who claim that AI systems were used to select people and homes for attack on a massive scale, with some insiders describing the process as 'insanely fun' and akin to a 'videogame.'
Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has called for the directors to be stripped of Israeli citizenship, accusing them of 'betrayal against the state.' item.title: Barcelona Confirms Andreas Christensen Will Miss Several Weeks With Quadriceps Injury
item.description:
FC Barcelona has confirmed that defender Andreas Christensen has suffered a muscle injury to the rectus femoris in his left quadriceps. The club announced that medical tests carried out on the Danish international confirmed the diagnosis following his injury during Barcelona’s match against Sevilla on Saturday.
Barcelona did not disclose the severity of the injury or provide a precise recovery timetable. However, the club stated that Christensen is expected to be sidelined for the next few weeks. His return to action will depend on how the injury develops during his recovery and rehabilitation.

item.description:
Uber Technologies Inc. has been ordered to pay $40 million to the parents of Emily Normandin-Parker, a 23-year-old woman who was fatally struck by a vehicle after an Uber driver left her and a friend stranded on a California freeway in August 2023. The incident occurred on State Route 73 in Orange County after the driver, Vu Tran, pulled over at an unsafe gore point following a dispute over a cleaning fee when one passenger became ill. According to the arbitration document, Tran showed no concern for Normandin-Parker's whereabouts despite knowing she had exited the vehicle while intoxicated. She subsequently wandered into traffic and was hit by a car traveling at 70 miles per hour.
The $40 million award was the outcome of a private arbitration process conducted in March 2026 by Richard A. Stone, a retired judge and arbitrator in Los Angeles. Napolitano, published on September 10, 2026, examines the constitutional implications of military actions taken by the U.S. government, particularly focusing on the unauthorized war against Iran. The article references historical precedents, such as the Supreme Court case Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. item.title: AI and Wear Analysis Reveal How Romans Played a Long-Lost Board Game
item.description:
For years, a small limestone slab covered with a grid of rectangles and lines sat unnoticed in a Dutch museum, dismissed by experts as mere architectural debris. Now, a study published in the journal Antiquity proposes that this 8-by-6-inch stone was actually a board for an ancient Roman game, and researchers believe they have reconstructed how it was played.
Using artificial intelligence to analyze microscopic wear patterns on the stone and running thousands of computer simulations, a team led by Walter Crist of Leiden University in the Netherlands says it has revived a forgotten recreational activity. The work not only suggests the rules of the game but also helps solve a long-standing archaeological puzzle about the artifact's purpose.
The Romans were enthusiastic gamers, even beyond the spectacles of the Colosseum. Ancient texts and excavated boards show a rich tradition of tabletop pastimes, including rota (similar to tic-tac-toe), us calculi (akin to Gomoku), and ludus latruncu

item.title: Group Portraits of Three Individuals in Late 19th and Early 20th Century Photography
item.description: The article discusses the conventions of group photography featuring three individuals during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It explains how studio photographers arranged subjects in structured compositions, often using pyramid or triangular formations with one person standing centrally in the background while two others sat in front. The article notes that due to technical limitations of the time, including long exposure times required for early photographic processes like daguerreotypes and ambrotypes, subjects typically maintained neutral expressions to avoid blurring. The text also mentions that photographers positioned subjects close together to convey familial connections while keeping everyone within the sharp focal plane of large-format lenses. The article provides historical context about Victorian and Edwardian era photography practices, highlighting how social etiquette and fashion trends influenced these group portrait conventions. item.description:
Voting has ended in Russia’s tightly controlled parliamentary elections, where President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party was widely expected to win by a substantial margin. item.title: Anthropic’s annualized revenue pace rises above $100 billion as it considers an IPO
item.description:
Anthropic is now on track to generate more than $100 billion in annual revenue, according to a report by The New York Times cited by Axios. The figure represents a 50% increase from the company’s reported revenue pace just two months earlier, highlighting the extraordinary speed of growth in the artificial intelligence sector.
The company’s expansion has been driven largely by strong enterprise adoption of its Claude Code and Cowork products. Its current revenue pace is reportedly more than ten times higher than it was at the end of 2025. If that trajectory continues, Anthropic could rank among the 50 largest U.S. companies by revenue before the end of 2026 and among the nation’s 10 largest companies by market capitalization.
Anthropic was founded only six years ago, making the scale of its growth particularly notable. The company is also continuing to pursue an initial public offering, despite ongoing debate about AI safety and the rapid development of advanced, or frontier, models.

item.title: AfD Wins Mecklenburg-Vorpommern State Election as CDU Suffers Historic Loss
item.description: Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the state election in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern with 38% of the vote, according to exit polls released on Sunday. The result marks another significant victory for the AfD, coming just two weeks after its historic win in Saxony-Anhalt, and intensifies pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. The CDU performed disastrously in the largely rural northeastern state, securing only 5% of the vote—barely enough to maintain representation and marking the party's worst state election result in 75 years. Chancellor Merz himself described the outcome as a 'disaster' while calling for reforms to address Germany's economic challenges and growing political divisions. AfD co-leader Alice Weidel celebrated the result, declaring her party 'clearly the new people's party in Germany' and calling for Merz's replacement. item.description: The article discusses a new book by Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Jill Lepore titled 'The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State,' which examines how digital infrastructure has increasingly taken control of democratic processes. Lepore, who previously won a Pulitzer for 'We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution,' explores the concept of the 'artificial state'—a digital communication infrastructure used by governments and corporations to automate and control public discourse. The book questions how democracy has ceded control to machines and whether it can be reclaimed. Lepore highlights the 2026 U.S. midterms as a pivotal moment, noting that this year marks the first AI election, where voters consult chatbots for voting advice and campaigns use AI for micro-targeted messaging, deepfakes, and tailored ads. item.title: Stanford Research Reveals Human Brain Comprises Two Evolutionarily Distinct Nervous Systems
item.description: New research led by Stanford Medicine has revealed that the human brain is not a single organ but rather consists of two distinct nervous systems that evolved independently over hundreds of millions of years. According to the study published in a Stanford University article, these two systems are the more primitive brainstem (responsible for regulating heart rate, breathing, and other autonomic functions) and the more advanced forebrain/midbrain (capable of complex cognitive functions such as poetry, mathematics, and self-reflection). The discovery explains why scientists have struggled for decades to grow certain types of brain cells in the laboratory, particularly hindbrain neurons, which follow a separate developmental pathway from the forebrain and midbrain. The researchers discovered that during embryonic development, the hindbrain follows a parallel developmental path rather than branching off from the forebrain/midbrain pathway. item.title: Delphin Enjolras: A Master of Elegant French Portraiture from the Early 20th Century
item.description: Delphin Enjolras (1857–1945) was a French academic painter renowned for his elegant and intimate depictions of women. Born in Coucouron in the Ardèche, Enjolras studied under prominent artists such as Jean-Léon Gérôme before developing his distinctive style. Initially focusing on landscapes, he transitioned to creating portraits and interior scenes featuring young women engaged in quiet, everyday activities such as reading, sewing, or resting, often illuminated softly by lamplight. Working primarily in oil, pastel, and watercolor, Enjolras produced refined, atmospheric works that captured moments of quiet elegance and grace. His paintings are celebrated for their delicate use of light, refined technique, and intimate mood, reflecting the refined aesthetic of early 20th-century French art. Notable works include 'Reading by Lamplight,' 'Portrait of a Woman in a Red Dress,' and 'Young Woman Reading by a Window.' item.description: Five California prisoners coordinated a lethal attack on a fellow inmate at Pelican Bay State Prison, according to officials. Rene B. He was pronounced dead at the prison clinic approximately one hour later. Surveillance footage revealed that Joseph W. Morales, 40, was convicted in 2019 for killing a man in Woodcrest, while Garcia, 52, has served a life sentence since 1997 after being found guilty of murder and assault in San Luis Obispo County. The footage also showed that Morales and Garcia handed weapons to Estevan Saucedo, who disposed of them in a garbage can. Two other inmates, Jose D. Rodriguez and Freddie G. During a recent appearance on 'The Daily Beast Podcast' with host Joanna Coles, Moran highlighted that Trump's dismissal of the cost-of-living crisis as a 'hoax' is alienating both traditional Republican voters and younger demographics. Moran emphasized that the crisis is pervasive, especially affecting farmers, who are grappling with rising diesel and fertilizer prices, which are exacerbated by geopolitical tensions involving Iran and the ongoing conflict between Ukraine and Russia. He noted that these economic pressures are causing staunch Republican voters, such as Iowa's farmers, to reconsider their support for Trump, as they face significant financial losses due to what Moran described as 'Trump inflation.' Rep. item.title: Study Links Common Food Preservatives to Increased Risk of Hypertension and Cardiovascular Disease
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in the European Heart Journal has identified eight common food preservatives associated with a higher risk of hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Conducted by researchers from the Nutritional Epidemiology Research Team at Université Sorbonne Paris Nord and Université Paris Cité, the study analyzed data from over 112,000 French participants over a period of seven to eight years. Participants recorded their dietary intake every six months through detailed three-day food diaries, allowing researchers to track consumption of specific preservatives. The findings revealed that individuals with the highest intake of non-antioxidant preservatives had a 29% higher risk of developing hypertension compared to those with the lowest intake, while also showing a 16% increased risk of cardiovascular disease. item.title: Claude Code's Shell Command Issues on macOS: Understanding the BSD vs. GNU Toolchain Conflict
item.description: The article discusses a common issue faced by macOS users who utilize Claude Code, an AI-powered coding assistant. The core problem is that Claude Code generates shell commands that fail on macOS due to fundamental differences between macOS's BSD-based toolchain and the GNU tools assumed by most shell examples. The author explains two primary reasons for this issue: first, Claude Code's 'Bash' tool actually runs the user's login shell (zsh on macOS since Catalina), not bash, causing subtle command behavior differences; second, macOS uses BSD versions of standard tools (like sed, date, and stat) rather than GNU versions, which have different syntax and options. The article details how common commands like 'sed -i' behave differently on BSD versus GNU systems, often leaving behind backup files or causing errors. The author provides a practical solution involving environment variables (CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL and CLAUDE_ENV_FILE) to force the use of GNU tools through Homebrew's coreutils packag

item.description: The article discusses a military expert's critique of President Donald Trump's proposal to militarize a planned Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C. Tom Nichols, a staff writer at The Atlantic and retired professor at the U.S. Navy War College, argues that Trump's plans to add sniper posts and drone technology to the arch are not only un-American but also reveal the 'darkness' surrounding the president. Nichols points out that militarizing the arch in front of the Memorial Bridge would create dangerous traffic patterns that could be exploited by terrorists, as the area already has numerous choke-points. The arch's proximity to Reagan National Airport would add unnecessary security challenges to an already overburdened facility. Nichols also notes that the project's symbolism is offensive to American values, comparing it to the Russian Kremlin and Napoleon's Arc de Triomphe, which celebrated foreign conquests. item.description: The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold represents a steady evolution in the foldable smartphone market rather than a revolutionary leap. Google has chosen to focus on refining the software experience and AI integration rather than making significant hardware upgrades. The device features a Tensor G6 chip with 16GB of RAM and up to 1TB of storage, delivering smooth performance for most users, though it doesn't match the raw power of competitors in high-end gaming or heavy photography. The phone boasts an IP68 rating for durability, a thinner and lighter design, and a nearly unbreakable back glass. A notable improvement is the 6.5-inch glass-ceramic cover screen with thinned bezels, making the foldable experience more intuitive for new users. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold introduces 'App Handles,' a feature allowing users to pin apps to the taskbar for flexible window management, similar to OnePlus Open's Open Canvas. item.title: Home Loan Comparison Can Save Borrowers Thousands Over 30-Year Term
item.description: According to a recent survey by LendingTree, an online lending platform, only 66 percent of homebuyers compared mortgage rates from multiple lenders, and just 54 percent negotiated with their lenders. This lack of comparison shopping results in significant missed savings, with borrowers missing out on an average of $62,572 over the course of a 30-year loan. The Washington Post article highlights that while consumers routinely comparison shop for items like shoes and sweaters, they often overlook the importance of comparing mortgage options. The article emphasizes that taking the time to shop around for the best home loan rates can lead to substantial long-term savings, potentially amounting to $60,000 or $120,000 over the life of the loan. The piece, written by Michele Lerner and published on September 20, 2026, underscores the financial benefits of being proactive in the mortgage process. item.title: Three Young People Killed, One Injured in Speeding BMW Crash on Mumbai's Coastal Road
item.description: A BMW crashed on Mumbai's Coastal Road near Lotus Jetty on Sunday morning around 5:20 a.m., resulting in the deaths of three individuals and leaving one critically injured. According to police reports, the vehicle was traveling from Marine Drive towards Haji Ali when the driver allegedly lost control due to overspeeding. The car struck a boundary wall before plunging off the bridge. The deceased victims have been identified as Shanay Gajjal (21) and Dhirya Seth (17), while a 25-year-old man was also declared dead upon arrival at the scene. The fourth occupant, an unidentified male aged approximately 20, sustained severe injuries and is currently in critical condition in the hospital's trauma ward. The Mumbai Coastal Road is a 10.58-kilometer high-speed freeway connecting Marine Drive in south Mumbai to the Worli end of the Bandra–Worli Sea Link. item.title: Tropical Storm Fay Forms Near the Azores but Currently Poses No Threat to Land
item.description:
Tropical Storm Fay formed in the northern Atlantic on the morning of Sunday, September 20, 2026, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. The storm was located approximately 450 miles southwest of the Azores, a group of nine Portuguese islands in the North Atlantic Ocean.
Fay had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph, placing it within the tropical-storm category rather than hurricane status. Tropical storms have sustained winds between 39 and 73 mph, while hurricanes require winds of at least 74 mph. Some additional strengthening was expected in the short term, but forecasters indicated that Fay was likely to weaken and dissipate later in the week.
At the time of the report, Fay posed no threat to land, and no coastal watches or warnings were in effect. The storm was also roughly 2,400 miles from the U.S. East Coast, making significant effects on the United States unlikely. item.title: BBC News Presenter Maryam Moshiri Shares Journey with Incurable Blood Cancer Diagnosis
item.description: Maryam Moshiri, a BBC News presenter, has publicly shared her experience with an incurable blood cancer diagnosis, polycythaemia vera (PV), which she was diagnosed with in November 2024. PV, also known as erythrocytosis, is a rare blood cancer that causes the body to produce too many red blood cells, with no known cure but manageable through treatment. Moshiri, 49, revealed she has been living with the condition for two years and has come to understand its physical and psychological impact. She emphasized that while the prognosis is good with proper medication, she will require lifelong medical care. Moshiri described the emotional struggle of accepting her diagnosis, including initial feelings of self-pity and guilt, as she realized she would need to manage the condition for the rest of her life. item.title: NHTSA Works on Standardized Testing for Autonomous Vehicle Safety
item.description: The article discusses the ongoing challenges in determining when autonomous vehicles (AVs) are safe enough for public roads. Currently, there is no standardized test for evaluating automated driving systems in real-world conditions, unlike the driver's license test required for humans. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is working on a federal automated vehicle framework to establish safety standards without stifling innovation. A key step in this process is the agreement with SAE to launch ASCEND, a government-industry initiative aimed at developing data-driven AV performance standards. NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison emphasized the importance of ADS (Automated Driving System) competency standards to address inconsistent state and local regulations. item.description: On June 30, 2026, Lawfare Daily featured a conversation with Cory Doctorow, a science fiction author, activist, journalist, and adviser to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, about his new book 'The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI.' The discussion covered whether the AI bubble will burst or merely deflate, the unit economics behind it, the concept of the 'reverse centaur' where workers serve machines, and how this maps onto broader cultural issues including AI 'knowledge collapse,' the human equivalent of AI model collapse. item.title: NIST Experiment Reveals Persistent Discrepancy in Measurement of Gravitational Constant
item.description: After a decade-long experiment, scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have measured the universal gravitational constant (G) with unprecedented precision, but their results differ from a previous French measurement by 0.0235%. The discrepancy, though small, deepens a 225-year-old physics puzzle that has challenged scientists since the time of Isaac Newton. The NIST team, led by physicist Stephan Schlamminger, employed a torsion balance method similar to Henry Cavendish's 1798 experiment, using copper and sapphire masses to rule out material-related errors. To eliminate bias, they blinded the experiment by scrambling data and sealing the correction factor in an envelope, only opening it after two years of additional analysis to account for air pressure effects. item.title: United Nations Marks International Day for Nuclear Disarmament Amid Growing Global Concerns
item.description: The United Nations commemorates September 26 as the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, highlighting the ongoing challenges in achieving global nuclear disarmament. Established by the General Assembly in 1946, this day serves as a reminder of the UN's long-standing commitment to eliminating nuclear weapons, which has been a priority since the organization's inception. Despite significant progress in reducing deployed nuclear arsenals since the Cold War, the world still faces a critical situation: an estimated 12,187 nuclear weapons remain in existence, with many nations actively modernizing their arsenals. The withdrawal of the United States from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in 2019 and Russia's suspension of participation in the New START treaty in 2023 have further strained the international arms control framework. Host Peter Doocy challenged Hassett with polling data showing only 23% of voters describe the economy as 'excellent or good,' 12% feel financially secure, and 62% view grocery prices as a major family concern. Hassett then conceded that prices are high but blamed the previous Biden administration for inherited inflation, stating 'we had 20% inflation under Joe Biden' and that inflation has 'way down over the last three months.' item.title: 18th-Century Medical Innovation: Fabric Womb Mannequin Revolutionized Childbirth Training
item.description: In the 18th century, childbirth was a perilous event with high mortality rates for both mothers and infants due to limited medical knowledge and lack of skilled care. Angélique Marguerite Le Boursier du Coudray, born in 1712, emerged as a pioneering midwife who transformed childbirth practices through education and innovation. With royal support from King Louis XV in 1759, she embarked on a nationwide mission to train rural midwives and surgeons, traveling extensively to teach practical childbirth techniques. Her most significant contribution was the invention of a life-sized fabric and leather birthing mannequin, which allowed medical students to practice procedures in a realistic yet safe environment. This innovation marked one of the earliest applications of simulation in medical education, significantly improving maternal care quality. item.title: Coral Cilia Function Fails in Warmer Waters, Threatening Reef Survival
item.description: Corals, often mistaken for colorful rocks, are complex organisms that form colonies and require oxygen to survive. Recent research published in Science in May 2026 reveals a critical aspect of coral physiology: the role of microscopic hairlike cilia in oxygen management. These cilia, previously overlooked, generate vortices of water to circulate oxygen to coral tissues, especially at night when symbiotic algae stop photosynthesizing. However, as ocean temperatures rise, the cilia's function becomes compromised. Warmer water holds less oxygen, prompting corals to increase cilia movement to compensate. At temperatures above 37°C (98.6°F), the cilia begin to slow down, and at 39°C (102.2°F), they cease entirely, leading to coral suffocation and death. The study, conducted by researchers from the University of Copenhagen and MIT, involved exposing coral to incremental temperature increases up to 39°C in controlled aquarium settings. Hiller challenges the notion of 'Swedish Death Cleaning,' a trend where individuals meticulously sort through their belongings before death, advocating instead for a more relaxed approach. item.title: NASA's Discarded Spacecraft Debris Creates Craters on Mars, Revealing Surface Weakness
item.description: NASA's Mars 2020 mission, which delivered the Perseverance rover to the Martian surface, inadvertently created five craters when it jettisoned two tungsten cruise ballast mass devices (CBMDs) and fragments from the cruise stage. These CBMDs, weighing 77 kilograms each, and the 540-kilogram cruise stage fragments impacted Mars at a velocity of 4.7 kilometers per second, creating craters approximately 70 kilometers northwest of Jezero crater. The craters were identified using images from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which captured the new impact sites that were absent in pre-2020 imagery. Researchers analyzed the craters using models to determine the surface properties of Mars, finding that the material is far weaker than predicted by standard crater-scaling laws. The cohesion strength was measured at around 7 kilopascals, comparable to sandy material that can be easily compressed. The deficit has ballooned from an estimated $7.5 billion to $27 billion within months, coinciding with President Zelensky's 40-day military campaign against Russia that triggered a significant escalation. Ukrainian officials, including Finance Minister Sergey Marchenko, have warned of 'liquidity issues' and potential delays in payments for non-military services, with the risk of repeating the 2022 financial crisis. Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky acknowledged 'exceptionally difficult challenges,' including the $27 billion defense hole and the risk of losing access to a $29.5 billion tranche of Western funding contingent on government reforms. The EU has been reluctant to acknowledge the $27 billion figure, instead calling for technica

item.title: One year after Gus Lamont disappeared, Australian police still have no answers
item.description:
Four-year-old Gus Lamont disappeared from his grandparents’ remote sheep station in South Australia on September 27, 2025, triggering the largest police search in the state’s history. Gus was last seen playing outside the family home, about 30 miles from the nearest town. His family began searching the property after realizing he was missing, and police were called as daylight faded.
Hundreds of police officers, military personnel, volunteers and specialist search teams subsequently examined a large area surrounding the property. Investigators searched buildings, dams and abandoned mine shafts, used helicopters, drones, thermal imaging and dogs, and later expanded the aerial search zone to hundreds of square miles. High-resolution aerial imagery was also analyzed with artificial intelligence. Despite the extensive effort, investigators found no clothing, personal belongings or other physical evidence that could establish what happened to Gus.

item.title: AI Industry Giants Fear Competition More Than Their Products, Says Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow, a tech columnist, argues that major AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta are not genuinely concerned about the risks of their AI products but are instead terrified of the intense competition among themselves. These companies, which he refers to as 'hyperscalers,' are engaged in a costly race to develop increasingly advanced AI models, spending billions on infrastructure and research. Doctorow contends that the business model of these companies is fundamentally flawed, as they are losing money with every new customer and every new use of their products, and their unit economics are negative. Despite claims of imminent profitability, the evidence supporting this is weak, and there are indications that companies are manipulating financial metrics to appear profitable. Doctorow highlights that AI chatbots have very low switching costs, meaning customers can easily switch from one provider to another, which creates a 'Red Queen's race' where companies must co

item.title: US Navy Outlines Technology Priorities for Future Procurement
item.description:
The US Navy has released a detailed list of technology priorities for the next several years, outlining five key areas where it plans to focus its procurement efforts. Justin Fanelli, the Department of Navy's Chief Technology Officer, discussed these priorities during a recent interview, emphasizing the Navy's shift toward streamlining procurement processes and collaborating more closely with commercial technology providers. The Navy aims to move away from traditional 'spaghetti chart' entry points for startups toward a more efficient funnel system that identifies and integrates successful companies into its technology base.
Fanelli explained that while the Navy spends approximately $150 billion annually on procurement, it is increasingly seeking co-investment opportunities with private capital rather than relying solely on traditional prime contractors. The focus has shifted to purchasing from Series D through F stage companies, rather than funding early-stage research internally. Th

item.title: Trump Proposes Executive Order to Centralize Health Research Funding Oversight
item.description: According to a Politico report cited by Reuters, U.S. President Donald Trump is seeking to bring a major part of national funding for health research under the control of his political appointees. The proposed arrangement would involve directing his budget director, Russ Vought, to draft an executive order creating a board that would determine which grants are funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH). The board would include NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya and Vought, the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, and would require unanimous decisions on grant awards. This move would give Vought a direct role in determining how the health research agency distributes its congressionally-appropriated funds. The Office of Management and Budget, the White House, and the Health and Human Services Department did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment outside regular business hours. The reported initiative comes amid growing criticism of the U.S. gove

item.title: Measles exposure warning issued after infected Amtrak rider travels through six California counties
item.description:
California public health officials have issued a warning about potential measles exposure across six counties after an unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state on Amtrak trains and connecting buses. The infected individual arrived in Los Angeles from Chicago on September 10, 2026, and subsequently traveled through Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento, and San Joaquin counties before departing for Denver on September 14.
Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that poses the greatest risk to unvaccinated individuals, especially young children and pregnant people. According to the California Department of Public Health, passengers who were on the same trains or buses, or who were present at the stations during the specified times, may have been exposed to the virus.
As of September 14, 2026, California has reported 59 measles cases across 13 counties, with 94 percent of patients either unvaccinated or having unknown vaccination status. Health officials emphasize

item.title: El Incidente Vela: Israel y Sudáfrica (probablemente) detonaron una bomba nuclear en el Océano Índico
item.description:
El Incidente Vela, también conocido como el Incidente de la Bomba Nuclear de 1979, es un evento histórico que ha generado controversia y especulación durante décadas. En 1979, un satélite estadounidense detectó una explosión nuclear en el Océano Índico, cerca de la costa de Sudáfrica. La detección fue realizada por el sistema de monitoreo de explosiones nucleares de los Estados Unidos, que registró una señal de radiación que indicaba una detonación de una bomba nuclear de aproximadamente 200 kilotones. La ubicación de la explosión, cerca de la costa de Sudáfrica, sugirió que podría haber sido un ensayo nuclear realizado por un país que no era parte del Tratado de No Proliferación Nuclear (NPT).
Durante años, se especuló que Israel y Sudáfrica podrían haber colaborado en un ensayo nuclear secreto. Israel, que no es parte del NPT y ha mantenido una política de ambigüedad nuclear, y Sudáfrica, que en ese momento estaba bajo el régimen del apartheid y tenía un programa nuclear en desarrol

item.title: Bundibugyo Virus Outbreak Highlights Gaps in Global Health Preparedness
item.description: A growing outbreak of the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda is drawing attention to the challenges of preparing for rare but deadly viral diseases. The Bundibugyo virus, a relative of Ebola belonging to the filovirus family, has caused 695 confirmed cases and 138 deaths as of June 11, 2026, surpassing previous outbreaks in both scale and trajectory. According to a review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine by Boston University professor Nancy Sullivan, the current outbreak underscores critical gaps in global health preparedness. Sullivan emphasizes that outbreak response requires rapid diagnosis, isolation of infected patients, contact tracing, strengthened infection control, and supportive medical care. However, in regions with limited laboratory resources, delays in confirming infections can significantly hinder containment efforts. The virus causes severe hemorrhagic fever, with symptoms that often overlap with more common ill

item.title: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy Before Philadelphia Concert as Supporting Acts Withdraw
item.description:
Ed Sheeran returned to the stage in Philadelphia on Saturday night for his first performance since the controversy surrounding the removal of Macklemore from his U.S. tour dates. Before beginning his show at Lincoln Financial Field, Sheeran addressed the situation directly, expressing regret over the decision to cut Macklemore after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments during a previous concert. Sheeran explained that he has been deeply affected by the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict and faced difficult choices that ultimately thrust him into a political debate he had not sought.
Following Macklemore's exit, several other supporting acts, including Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and the Danish band Lukas Graham, also withdrew from the tour over the past week. Sheeran condemned the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel as horrific while also describing Israel's military response in Gaza as catastrophic and disproportionate. He emphasized that his concerts should remain a san

item.title: Hot Beverages Linked to Increased Esophageal Cancer Risk, Study Finds
item.description: A recent study published in The Financial Express highlights a significant health concern regarding the consumption of very hot beverages. According to Dr. Akshat Malik, senior consultant in head and neck oncology at Apollo Hospital in Delhi, drinking tea and other hot beverages at temperatures above 65°C is associated with a tripled risk of developing esophageal cancer. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified such beverages as 'probably carcinogenic to humans' due to evidence linking repeated thermal injury to the esophageal lining. Dr. Malik emphasizes that while the reported risk increase should not be interpreted as a fixed three-fold increase for every individual, it is advisable to allow hot drinks to cool to a comfortable temperature before consumption. The article also addresses common questions about esophageal health, explaining that temperature is particularly relevant for direct irritation of the esophageal lining, while spicy foods work differ

item.title: Restoring Brain Protein Menin Reverses Aging Signs in Mice, Study Shows
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in PLOS Biology on March 16, 2023, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University, has identified a key brain protein called Menin that plays a significant role in aging. Researchers discovered that declining levels of Menin in the hypothalamus, a small brain region regulating metabolism, contribute to systemic aging effects including inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. The study demonstrated that restoring Menin in older mice reversed several age-related changes, improving skin thickness, bone mass, and cognitive performance. Additionally, the amino acid D-serine, which is involved in brain signaling, was found to improve cognition when administered separately. However, D-serine supplementation did not replicate the broader physical improvements seen with Menin restoration. Subsequent research has further explored the connection between Menin, brain inflammation, and aging. A 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry

item.title: Five dead after SUV hits LA Metro bus and news helicopter crashes during coverage
item.description:
A deadly chain of events unfolded in Chatsworth, Los Angeles, on Tuesday night when an SUV driven by an allegedly intoxicated woman crashed into a Metro bus, killing two passengers. Just two hours later, an NBC4 news helicopter covering the scene crashed less than a mile away, killing the reporter, the pilot, and a Guatemalan tourist on the ground. In total, five people died in the twin tragedies that shocked the community.
Authorities identified the bus crash victims as Gage Weida, 31, who was days away from his 32nd birthday, and Daniel Castillo, 46, a father of four. The SUV driver, Bailee Lynn Rios, faces second-degree murder, DUI, and reckless driving charges after allegedly running a red light at high speed while under the influence of drugs. She was hospitalized and later appeared in court on a stretcher, with bail set at $4.1 million.
The helicopter crash occurred as NBC4's Ana Moreno and veteran pilot George Marciniw were providing aerial coverage of the bus collision. Video

item.title: Trump Proposes New Name for AI and Announces AI Force
item.description: President Donald Trump has made several statements regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in recent days, declaring that concerns about AI safety are part of a 'hoax' orchestrated by Democrats. On Truth Social, Trump posted a poll asking followers to vote on a new name for AI, with options including 'Superior Intelligence,' 'Extreme Intelligence,' and 'Supreme Intelligence.' He also claimed that attempts to 'decimate or destroy AI' are part of a broader pattern of Democratic 'hoaxes,' similar to previous issues like 'Russia, Russia, Russia' and 'Global Warming.' Trump stated he would 'cherish' the AI industry, help it grow, and establish an 'AI Force,' similar to the Space Force he created during his first term. He also mentioned appointing an 'AI Czar' for high-IQ individuals. The president's comments come amid heightened debate over AI safety, following an AI researcher's resignation from Anthropic over concerns about AI's potential existential threats. item.title: Flock Safety Offers Voluntary Buyouts to Prevent Layoffs Amid Customer Losses
item.description: Flock Safety, a company specializing in license plate recognition technology, is offering voluntary buyouts to employees to avoid layoffs as it faces significant customer losses. According to reports from WIRED and Mashable, the company has experienced a substantial decline in contracts, with many city and county governments cutting ties in 2026. In August alone, 93 local governments terminated agreements with Flock, representing roughly three times as many as the previous five years combined. The company's financial struggles are compounded by a wave of vandalism targeting its cameras, which has increased operational costs unexpectedly. Flock has raised approximately $1.2 billion in venture capital but is now facing revenue shortfalls that could necessitate staff reductions. The buyout program aims to allow employees to depart voluntarily, potentially avoiding the need for involuntary layoffs. item.title: Accessory Dwelling Units Offer Housing Solutions and Additional Income for Homeowners
item.description: Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) are gaining popularity as a practical solution for homeowners seeking to maximize their property's potential. These units, which can be attached or detached structures on the same property as an existing home, such as an apartment above a garage or a standalone small house, provide additional living space and generate rental income. The Washington Post article highlights Pavel Kazenkov, owner of Capital ADU, who built an ADU on his Petworth property in Northwest Washington. Kazenkov and his wife purchased their home in 2018 and recognized the potential of their deep lot to accommodate an ADU. The article emphasizes that ADUs not only offer homeowners extra room but also contribute to easing housing shortages in certain regions. By creating additional rental units, ADUs help address the growing demand for affordable housing, particularly in urban areas where space is limited.
